questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The room and the single vanishing point of the Last Supper
questions.learningObjective: account for a unified architectural space on a wall that was not painted wet
questions.stem: A wall painting made between 1495 and 1498 in the refectory of a convent church in Milan shows twelve men at a long table, arranged in four groups of three behind it, in a room with a coffered ceiling, side walls hung with tapestries, and windows on the left. The lines of the ceiling coffers, the tops of the tapestries and the edges of the table all converge on a single point behind the head of the central figure. The wall was painted in tempera and oil on dry plaster rather than on wet. What does the convergence of all those lines establish?

options.text: That one measurable space contains the whole scene, so the room the viewer is in and the room in the painting are the same kind of room
That the figures are arranged by rank, since groups of three are a conventional way of ranking twelve people in a hierarchy
options.misconception: reads a spatial grouping as a statement about social precedence

options.text: That the painter had measured the refectory and copied it, since a room of this kind can only be drawn on the spot
options.misconception: supposes an architect's accuracy is required and that a constructed room must be measured

options.text: That the work was painted as a fresco, since a unified perspective is achievable only in a medium that binds to plaster
options.misconception: confuses a choice of geometry with a constraint imposed by the technique

questions.explanation: The point of the convergence is a single, checkable space. Ceiling coffers, tapestry tops, table edges and window heads are independent sets of parallel lines in the real world, and if they all meet at one point in the picture, then everything in the picture is in one room at one scale. That is a claim, not an impression: a viewer standing in the refectory can compare the painted room with the room they are in and find the same proportions and the same eye level, and that comparison is the strongest possible confirmation that a constructed space is a real one. The grouping of the figures follows from it rather than the other way round. Four groups of three are what twelve people become when they are placed in a room and allowed to react to one another across it, and the pairs that lean together and the pairs that turn away are the consequence of the space rather than a code for status. Two of the distractors confuse the geometry with something else. A group of three is not a rank; ranking in a painting of this kind is conveyed by gesture and placement, and the two men who pull back from the group that discusses a piece of bread are not outranked, they are dismayed. And the medium tells us nothing about the geometry: the wall here was painted on dry plaster in tempera and oil, which is a choice about drying time and about the modelling of faces, and a dry surface is if anything easier to draw on precisely because it can be corrected. The third error is the common one of assuming an invented room must be a measured one.
questions.hint: Ask what four independent sets of lines meeting at one point let a viewer check.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The parapet and the distant shores of the Mona Lisa
questions.learningObjective: explain how a foreground barrier and aerial perspective divide a picture's zones
questions.stem: An oil portrait on a poplar panel begun about 1503 in Florence and now in the Louvre shows a seated woman behind a plain parapet whose top edge runs straight across the picture at about the level of her hands. Beyond her, on the left, a road descends towards a rocky coast and a stretch of water; on the right the ground falls away in a series of folds to a second, differently lit stretch of water. What do the parapet and the two distant shores do?

options.text: They prove the sitter is outdoors, since a parapet with land falling away on both sides can only stand at a window
options.misconception: reads a painted barrier as evidence about a setting the picture does not describe

options.text: They show the picture is unfinished, since the two distant shores disagree in tone and a finished landscape would use one light
options.misconception: reads a deliberate contrast in distance as an inconsistency in the lighting

options.text: They identify the sitter, since a marble parapet of that form is a known studio device for disguising a plain room
options.misconception: treats a compositional device as evidence about a particular person's identity

options.text: They establish three zones with different kinds of space, so the figure is cut off from the distance rather than dissolved into it

questions.explanation: The parapet is the hinge of the whole picture, and its function is separation. A straight horizontal edge across the field, set at about the level of the sitter's hands, establishes a near zone and stops the eye at a boundary the viewer cannot cross, so the figure is read as present at a distance from a spectator who is behind that boundary. Behind her, the picture then opens into distance by a different route: not a single recession but two, one on each side, and the two are not the same. On the left a road, a coast and a stretch of water lie in cool, softened tones; on the right the ground falls in folds to water that is warmer and hazier. Two zones of distance rather than one is what keeps the space from reading as a stage flat, and it is also what makes the barrier necessary. The sharp edge of the parapet and the insubstantial distance beyond it are two different kinds of space held in the same frame, and the contrast between them is the picture's subject as much as the sitter is. Two errors to reject. A painted parapet is a construction, and it does not establish that the figure is outdoors; the same device is used in front of a plain interior wall in order to introduce a distance. And a device is not evidence about a person, however characteristic it is. The fourth is a failure of method: a two-zone landscape uses contrast on purpose, since a single uniform light would flatten the difference that makes the distance legible. The test: ask where the eye stops, and then ask what it is allowed to pass.
questions.hint: Ask what a straight edge across the field does, and why there are two distances rather than one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The sling and the absent helmet of the marble David
questions.learningObjective: account for a sculpture's attributes as the argument for its subject
questions.stem: A marble figure of about 1501 to 1504, some five metres high, was cut by Michelangelo for a cathedral in Florence and is now in the Galleria dell'Accademia. It shows a young man standing with all his weight on the right leg, the left leg forward with the heel raised and the toes down, a sling held in the left hand with a stone in the palm, the head turned and the brows drawn, and no crown. What do the sling, the stone and the absence of a crown do?

options.text: They fix the subject before the victory, since a sling, a stone and no crown describe a contest that is about to be decided
They show the figure is a portrait, since a turned head and a drawn brow are the standard signs of a living sitter
options.misconception: treats a specific expression as evidence that a named person sat for the figure

options.text: They show the figure is a river god, since a nude youth with a water-bearer in one hand is a common type in Florentine sculpture
options.misconception: supplies a classical type that the attributes contradict

options.text: They show the figure is unfinished, since a sculptor of this quality would have carved the sling strap, the stone and the hair together
options.misconception: reads deliberate concentration on the head and hands as an abandoned state

questions.explanation: The attributes are the argument, and they are arranged so that the argument is about a moment rather than a state. A sling over the shoulder, a stone resting in the palm of the extended left hand, and a face with the brows drawn and the lips shut describe a boy who is concentrating, in the instant before he moves, on an act whose outcome the viewer already knows. The absence of a crown removes the settled triumph from the figure and puts the contest in the future. The whole body agrees: the weight on one leg, the heel lifted and the toes down, is the stance of someone about to push off, and the twist that runs from the toes through the hip and shoulder to the turned head means the body and the attention are aimed at different things at once, which is exactly the condition of aiming. Everything the sculptor did not finish is consistent with this. The hair, the sling strap and the surface of the legs were not completed, and that is not a failure: they are the parts that are not involved in the moment, while the head, the hands and the twist carry the whole of the meaning. Three errors to reject. Concentrating effort where the meaning is, and leaving the rest, is a decision and not an abandonment. A specific expression is not a portrait, and no sitter is claimed. And a water-bearer in one hand would make the figure a river god of a familiar kind, which is precisely the alternative that the sling, the stone and the missing crown are there to refuse: the commission wanted a young Florentine before Florence's archangel, not a classical type.
questions.hint: Ask whether the figure is shown winning or about to begin winning, and what that does to the attributes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two vertical movements of the Last Judgment fresco
questions.learningObjective: read a monumental figure scheme as a movement rather than a list
questions.stem: A fresco painted between 1536 and 1541 on the end wall of a chapel in Rome shows a central figure with the arms out and the head bowed, two flanking bands of attendant figures, a field of nude bodies below, and on one side a crowd rising and being lifted and on the other a crowd falling and weighed. What does the division into a rising side and a falling side make the field of bodies into?

options.text: A catalogue, since each figure represents a particular person and the scheme is meant to be read figure by figure
options.misconception: turns a collective scheme into an enumerated list of sainted individuals

options.text: A correction, since the lower field was repainted twice and the two sides show the two states of the argument
options.misconception: supplies a history of repainting that the composition does not need

options.text: A single movement, so a hundred and fifty figures are read as one current split at the centre rather than as a list of individuals
A second subject, since the two sides show two different events separated by the central figure rather than one event divided
options.misconception: splits a continuous scheme into two independent narratives

questions.explanation: The scale of the field is the first fact. There are something in the order of a hundred and fifty figures in the lower zone, and at that number the eye cannot take individuals in one at a time, so it takes currents instead: bodies ascending on one side, bodies descending on the other, and the whole field swinging about the central figure. That is what makes the fresco monumental rather than crowded. A monumental scheme works by scale and direction, and the direction here is legible from the bottom of the wall: figures lower down are heavier, more contorted and moving the wrong way, and figures higher up are lighter, assisted and moving up, so the composition is read as a gradient before any face is examined. The two attendant bands at the sides are there to hold the middle of the wall together, and the band above the central figure continues the vertical axis upward. Two further features follow from reading it as one movement. The nudity is uniform, which is what lets the eye read the field as a single substance rather than as a crowd of individuals in costume. And the compression at the centre is deliberate: the bodies of the saved and the damned press towards each other under the lowered head, so the decisive point of the composition is a narrowing, not a display. The three errors each substitute a different logic. A catalogue would need the figures to be individuated, and they are not. Two subjects would need the sides to be independent, and they are mirror images of one condition. And a correction narrative is invented from a large number of figures, which needs no such history to be dense.
questions.hint: Ask whether the eye can take a hundred and fifty bodies one at a time, and what it takes instead.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The pair at the centre of the School of Athens
questions.learningObjective: explain how two gestures establish a subject without a label
questions.stem: A fresco painted between 1509 and 1511 in a room in the Vatican shows two men at the head of a broad staircase in the middle of a barrel-vaulted hall built of painted architecture, with about fifty other figures in groups below and around them. The one on the left holds a book and points down with his right hand; the one on the right holds a book and extends his hand palm-up. Every receding line of the architecture, the steps and the pavement meets at a single point between the two. What are the two gestures doing?

options.text: Fixing two opposed positions, so a book, a downward finger and an open palm set one claim against another without a label
Naming two philosophers, since a painter of this kind wrote the identity of a figure on the stone beside him
options.misconception: relies on written names, which this fresco has none of

options.text: Establishing rank, since the pair stand alone on the steps while everyone else is arranged below them in a graded society
options.misconception: reads a compositional hierarchy as a claim about the standing of real people

options.text: Balancing the picture, since a large hall with many figures must have an even number of focal points or the eye has nowhere to rest
options.misconception: proposes a rule about even focal points that this fresco does not observe

questions.explanation: Two hands are doing the identifying, and the argument is that no labels are needed. The figure on the left holds a book and points downward, which is a gesture about the world of change and sense; the one on the right holds a book too and opens his hand outward and upward, which is a gesture about the unmoved and the general. So one book and one argument, set side by side and made to look like two answers to the same question, and the picture's whole subject is that opposition. Everything else in the fresco is built to make that opposition legible. The staircase lifts the pair above the rest, the groups below them are arranged in conversation and in dispute, and the architecture exists to put them at the end of a corridor of lines whose convergence falls exactly in the gap between them, so the perspective itself declares that the space between these two is what the painting is about. That is the strongest possible compositional claim, and it is made without a single word. Two of the distractors ask for evidence the fresco does not supply. There are no written names on the stones or the floor of this hall; the identifications are proposals, argued from the gestures, the books, the company each figure keeps and the settings they stand in, and a good answer should say that they are proposals. A graded arrangement of figures is also not a claim about real standing, and the surrounding groups are not ranked but distributed by topic. The fourth answer offers a rule the fresco breaks: it has one focal point, not two, and the single point between the figures is what the eye is taken to.
questions.hint: Ask what a downward finger and an open palm each claim, and what the single vanishing point is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The interrupted marble background of a Florentine double portrait
questions.learningObjective: explain what a partly executed ground reveals about a working method
questions.stem: An oil on wood of about 1506, now in the Uffizi, shows a young woman standing behind a carved marble parapet, with a relief of putti and figures in low relief behind her and a distant plain beyond. Her hands are held in a complicated turn at her waist, the knuckles of one hand showing and the wrist sharply foreshortened, and the air between her forearm and her face carries a faint shadow. The relief behind her is thin and sketchy while her head and hands are fully worked. What does the state of the background establish?

options.text: That the panel was damaged, since a thin relief with visible sketch lines is what is left after a layer of paint has been lost
options.misconception: reads a deliberately thin passage as chemical or physical loss

options.text: That the sitter's pose was corrected, since the twist of the waist and the foreshortened wrist are a pose no painter could draw from life
options.misconception: supplies a technical incapacity where a difficult pose was the aim

options.text: That the relief is a copy from a print, since shallow carving with a linear design is characteristic of a graphic source
options.misconception: infers a graphic origin from a handling that suits a background

options.text: That the figure was completed first and the setting afterwards, so the panel records a sequence of working rather than an accident

questions.explanation: A panel in a mixed state of completion is a document about working, and it should be read as a sequence rather than as a defect. Here the head and the hands are the most finished passages and the relief behind is thin, linear and unresolved, and the only explanation that fits is that the painter began where the meaning was. That is the head, which carries the likeness, and the hands, which carry the pose, and a pose this difficult, with the wrist turned so the knuckles show and the forearm thrown across the body, is not a thing to be settled after the ground is done. The air between the arm and the face is part of the same thinking: a faint shadow there is what separates a turned arm from a flat silhouette, and it is placed with the figure rather than with the room. The parapet and the relief are doing their job as a setting, and they are doing it thinly because they are not the subject. The distractors each turn a working state into something else. A thin background is not a loss; there is nothing under it to recover, and the sketch lines are drawing rather than ghosting. Nor does shallow relief in a setting imply a print, since a background is the last thing to need invention. And the last answer is exactly backwards: a pose that cannot be drawn from life is the reason to draw it, and the foreshortening is a demonstration that the artist could.
questions.hint: Ask which passages are finished and which are thin, and what that order says about the painter's priorities.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three tiers of figures in the Frari Assumption
questions.learningObjective: read a vertical figure scheme as a single upward movement
questions.stem: An altarpiece painted between 1516 and 1518 for a chapel in Venice and still in it, oil on panel, shows about sixty figures in a single tall field: a band of apostles and saints along the bottom, a swirling ring of figures and putti in the middle, and the Virgin rising at the top in a red mantle, above a group of clouds. The painted frame above her carries seraphim. What does the arrangement make of the panel?

options.text: One continuous ascent, since the tiers are joined by a circular movement and the eye is carried up to the single figure at the top
A ceiling seen from below, since a field of figures seen edge-on in an arch is what a viewer standing under a vault actually sees
options.misconception: supplies a viewpoint the panel's own geometry contradicts

options.text: An imitation of a mosaic, since a gold frame with seraphim and a ring of figures is a convention borrowed from Venice's mosaics
options.misconception: proposes a mosaic derivation for a scheme that the panel's own framing states

options.text: A catalogue of witnesses, since each of the sixty figures is a separate individual and the order of them is a list of importance
options.misconception: turns a continuous movement into an enumerated roll of sainted persons

questions.explanation: The scheme is a single movement, and the evidence is the ring. An altarpiece divided into stacked bands of equal width would read as three scenes; this one does not, because the middle band is not a row but a vortex, a spiral of bodies and putti that turns and carries the eye up out of the bottom register and into the cloud at the top. So the composition has one direction, and the top of it is occupied by a single figure whose mantle and whose position above the clouds make her the destination of everything below. The bottom register is the base of the current, and the seraphim in the gilded frame are the last thing the eye meets before it leaves the panel altogether, so the frame itself is part of the ascent. That is what the frame is doing: not enclosing a picture but continuing it. Two of the distractors substitute a different logic. Nothing here is a roll of individuals, and at sixty figures in a continuous spiral the eye has no use for an enumeration. A ceiling viewpoint is not available here either: the figures are seen frontally and the space they occupy is a painted field inside a frame, not an arch seen from below. The third answer is a curiosity rather than a reading; a gold frame with seraphim is a feature of this altarpiece's own design, and a claim about a borrowed convention has to be made from something other than the presence of gold. The test to apply: ask which way the eye moves, and how many times it is given a new thing to follow.
questions.hint: Ask whether the middle band is a row or a turn, and what happens at the top of the panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The viewpoint from the foot of the bed in the Venus of Urbino
questions.learningObjective: explain how a chosen viewpoint controls what a picture can disclose
questions.stem: An oil on canvas of 1534, now in the Uffizi, shows a reclining nude woman seen from near the foot of her bed, so that her head, her torso and her bent leg are foreshortened away from the viewer; behind her are two dark cassoni, a curtain drawn back, a small standing cupid holding a flame, and two dogs. What does the position of the viewer determine?

options.text: Who the woman is, since a viewpoint from the foot of a bed establishes that the picture is a private and therefore an honest scene
options.misconception: infers a sitter's identity and the picture's honesty from a chosen viewpoint

options.text: That the woman is asleep, since a reclining body foreshortened from below cannot be a waking one
options.misconception: claims an expressional state from a foreshortening that cannot carry it

options.text: What can be disclosed, since looking from the foot of the bed sets the body receding and makes the small figures behind legible as signs
The date of the canvas, since a viewpoint at the foot of a bed is a device recorded only in the sixteenth century
options.misconception: turns a compositional device into a chronological index

questions.explanation: A viewpoint is a licence, and the whole of what a picture can show follows from where it puts the spectator. Here the spectator is at the foot of the bed, which is why the body recedes: the head is smallest, the torso foreshortened, the bent leg thrown toward the viewer, and the whole figure is read in a direction that a frontal view would not allow. That direction is also what makes the room behind available. The two cassoni at the back, the drawn-back curtain and the small standing figure with a flame are all readable precisely because the eye is already travelling away from the near body along the axis the bed sets up. And they are legible as signs, not as furniture: the cupid, the dogs, the cassoni, the curtain and the basket of fruit in the far corner have each been read as a term in a vocabulary about marriage, and what makes that reading possible is the arrangement, which puts the small things directly behind the large one so that they are compared rather than merely seen. Two errors to reject. A viewpoint establishes a position, not a person, and it says nothing about how truthful a scene is; a picture is not made honest by the angle of the eye. Nor is a device a date. The third is a claim about expression that cannot be made: a foreshortened body has no expression of its own, and the picture is not about whether anyone is asleep. The useful test for any picture with a strong viewpoint: ask what the position lets the painter disclose that another position would have hidden.
questions.hint: Ask what a different position of the eye would have hidden, and why the small things are placed where they are.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The later alterations on the Feast of the Gods
questions.learningObjective: use a documented change on a finished painting as evidence about taste
questions.stem: A mythological painting of 1514, on panel, now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, shows a gathering of gods around a table on a flowered bank beside a stream of wine that runs out of the picture in the foreground, with a priest in a white robe at the right. About fifteen years later the same panel was painted over: drapery and a bush were added, and the bare legs and the seat of one figure were covered. What does that later intervention tell you that the earlier date does not?

options.text: That the panel was altered after completion, and that the alteration records a change in what could be shown in a painting made for a palace
That the earlier date is wrong, since a painter who covered his own work cannot have made it in the first place
options.misconception: treats a later alteration as evidence against the earlier execution

options.text: That the gods were being identified, since covering a leg changes which of them the figure must be
options.misconception: supposes a covering changes a figure's identity, when it changes only what is visible

options.text: That the panel was copied, since only a copyist adds to a finished painting in order to bring it up to date
options.misconception: confuses a documented campaign of alteration with the act of copying

questions.explanation: The record here is unusually clear, and the right way to use it is as evidence about a moment rather than about the object. The panel was completed in 1514, and about fifteen years later somebody painted over it. What was added, a length of drapery and a bush, covers the bare legs and the seat of one figure; what is therefore established is that a finished painting in a palace collection was judged to show more than it should. That is a fact about taste and about audience at a particular date, and it is the sort of fact that survives the loss of every document about the alteration, because the alteration is still there. It also tells you something about what an intervention of this kind is not. It is not evidence against the earlier execution, since covering a leg is an act done to a picture, not a claim about who made it. It does not change who the figures are, since identity in a scene of this kind is carried by attributes and by company rather than by which parts of a leg are visible. And it is not a copy: a copy reproduces a model, and what happened here added to the original surface rather than repeating it. The general point is worth keeping: a change made to a finished picture is a dated act with a motive, and the motive is usually about the picture's audience rather than about its maker. Where a date for the campaign is recorded, it can be used with some confidence; where it is not, the intervention is still evidence, just weaker evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what was added and what it covered, and what kind of judgement leads someone to add to a finished painting.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The unresolved subject of the Venetian canvas
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a formal reading from a subject that cannot be settled
questions.stem: A small oil on canvas painted in Venice about 1506 to 1508 and now in the Gallerie dell'Accademia shows a landscape with a river, trees and a hill, a broken plank bridge in the middle distance, a woman nursing a baby on the right, a soldier with a long staff on the left, and a bright shaft of light falling across the right half of the picture. No documentary record names the subject. Which reading is properly supported?

options.text: A single certain subject, since the two marginal figures and the broken bridge occur in only one narrative in the tradition
options.misconception: claims an iconographic match that a survey of candidate subjects has not established

options.text: A private one, since an undated canvas of this size was necessarily made for a private buyer and not for a church
options.misconception: infers a destination from the absence of a record

options.text: A formal one, since the picture's meaning can be described in terms of light, the two figures at the margins and the empty centre, whatever the subject turns out to be
No reading at all, since a picture without a documented subject cannot be described in any useful way
options.misconception: concludes that an undetermined subject makes description impossible

questions.explanation: An undetermined subject is not an undetermined picture, and this is the case that shows why. The composition can be described exactly: a shaft of light that takes the right half of the field and leaves the left in shadow, a river running into a distance, a plank bridge broken in the middle, a woman nursing at the right edge and a standing soldier with a staff at the left, and a great deal of empty ground between them. Those are observations, and they support real claims: that the light is the organising event, that the two figures are pushed to the margins so that the centre stays open, that the broken bridge and the darkened left half are in tension with the lit right half, and that the picture is organised so that something is about to happen or has just stopped. The subject itself has been argued over for centuries, and a large number of candidates have been proposed, none of which has been established. The method to keep is the one this picture teaches: describe the arrangement, state the claims the arrangement supports, and mark the subject as an open question rather than settling it. Three errors to reject. An undetermined subject does not make description useless, since the formal reading is the durable part. Nor has any single narrative been demonstrated, and a candidate subject should never be asserted as a fact. And the absence of a record tells us nothing about who the picture was for; the absence of a record is an absence of a record.
questions.hint: Ask what can be said about the arrangement that does not depend on knowing the story.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The foreshortened body in the Miracle of the Slave
questions.learningObjective: explain how a single foreshortened figure reorganises a large canvas
questions.stem: A very large oil on canvas of 1548 in the Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice, shows a crowd of about thirty figures packed into a deep space, a group of well-dressed men at the right, a group of men in turbans and robes at the left, a long pole rising diagonally through the middle, and one naked figure falling head first, seen from above and foreshortened, in the centre of the picture. What does the falling figure do to the composition?

options.text: It shows the canvas was too large, since a figure of that angle needs a support bigger than the room can hold
options.misconception: infers a practical limit on scale from an angle of foreshortening

options.text: It proves the figure is a correction, since an early version of the fall was painted in a different position and this one was added
options.misconception: supplies a pentimento without any evidence from the surface

options.text: It supplies the subject, since a foreshortened body is the only figure in a picture that can be shown falling with certainty
options.misconception: treats a foreshortening device as the only possible way to depict a fall

options.text: It breaks the horizontal of the crowd and makes the eye travel along a diagonal that ends at the point of impact

questions.explanation: One figure in a picture can reorganise the whole of it, and this is the clearest case in sixteenth-century Venice. The crowd is arranged in horizontal masses, two groups of spectators at the sides, and every one of those bodies is upright and at rest. Against that, a single nude body is dropped head first from the top of the picture, seen from above, foreshortened so that it is read at an angle to the surface rather than flat on it. The figure therefore supplies the diagonal that the rest of the picture lacks, and the eye follows it down to the ground in the middle. That is the compositional job, and it is done by position and angle: a body crossing the field at an angle is more disruptive than any amount of incident in the crowd. The crowd's parts also become legible as a consequence. The group at the right presses in and the group at the left gestures, and the pole rising through the middle is a vertical counterweight to a figure that is entirely diagonal, so the two together set the direction of the whole event. Three errors to reject. A foreshortening is a way of drawing, not a requirement, and a fall can be shown any number of other ways. Nor is a steep angle a practical limit on scale; a canvas this size exists and is not thereby too large. And there is no evidence of a correction here: nothing in the composition requires a claim about an earlier position, and a pentimento has to be found in the paint rather than assumed from the design. The test to apply: remove the falling figure mentally and see how much of the picture's direction survives.
questions.hint: Ask what direction the crowd itself has, and what the falling body adds to it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A monumental refectory painting and its scale
questions.learningObjective: infer a function from a painting's recorded size and setting
questions.stem: A painting of 1563, in oil on canvas and nearly seven metres wide, was made for the refectory of a Benedictine monastery on an island in the Venetian lagoon. It shows a feast with about a hundred and thirty figures in three tiers, with Christ small and off-centre at the middle level, a row of musicians in extravagant dress across the bottom, and columns dividing the field. What does the size establish?

options.text: A viewing distance, since a picture that wide is read from the length of a room, which is what fixes the scale of the figures and the size of the canvas
A subject, since a banquet with a hundred and thirty figures can only be the marriage at Cana and no other feast has that number of guests
options.misconception: infers a narrative from a crowd size

options.text: A price, since a canvas of that area is so expensive that only a monastery could have paid for it
options.misconception: infers wealth from surface area, which no commission record supports

options.text: A competition, since no one paints that large in a city of painters unless trying to outdo a neighbour
options.misconception: assumes rivalry from scale alone

questions.explanation: Size is a viewing condition, and it is the most useful thing about this record. A canvas nearly seven metres wide goes on a refectory wall above a long table, so it is seen by people sitting or standing some tens of feet away, along the room rather than straight on. That distance is what fixes the figure scale, because the figures have to be large enough to register at that range, and it is also what makes the three tiers necessary: a crowd of a hundred and thirty has to be stacked vertically to fit the proportion of the wall, and the row of musicians at the bottom is placed to occupy the zone nearest the diners, whose own heads would otherwise cover it. The columns dividing the field do the same work at intervals, giving a frieze an architecture so the eye can be measured against something. So the size explains the structure of the picture. Two of the distractors read the record as evidence of something it cannot carry. A crowd size does not identify a feast; the subject here was named in the commission. Nor does a large canvas prove who could afford it, since the price of a commission is set by agreement and by the number of hands at work on it, not by the area of the support. The fourth answer is an unforced inference: painters produce large works without competing, and no record here mentions a rival. The test to apply: for a painting of a known size, ask how far away the first person to see it stood, and most of its formal decisions fall out of the answer.
questions.hint: Ask how far away a picture of that width is seen, and what that distance forces.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The patterned dress and the impassive face of a court portrait
questions.learningObjective: explain how surface detail and withheld expression work together
questions.stem: A portrait painted about 1545, oil on panel, now in the Uffizi, shows a woman standing in an enormously elaborate dress of brocade and jewelled trim against a dark architectural background that includes a carved pilaster and an inscription in a frieze above. Her hands rest on a child's head, her face is turned very slightly, and there is no smile and no sign of embarrassment. Which description of the relation between the dress and the face is best supported?

options.text: That the dress overwhelms the face, since an elaborate costume is the standard way of subordinating a sitter to a court
options.misconception: assumes a fixed relation between costume and status that this reading of the face would not support

options.text: That the inscription is the subject, since words on a picture always take precedence over what is painted below them
options.misconception: gives an inscription priority over the image it is set into

options.text: That the two work together, since the dress spends everything on pattern while the face gives nothing away, and the picture is about the family rather than the mood
That the face is unfinished, since a painter who could achieve that pattern would certainly have modelled the flesh more warmly
options.misconception: infers incomplete painting from a mismatch in warmth of handling

questions.explanation: The two passages of the panel are worked at opposite temperatures, and the contrast is the point. The dress is described at extraordinary length: the pattern of the brocade, the jewelled trim, the shape of the sleeve, the fall of the fabric, all of it drawn with a fine and even hand so that the surface reads as an expensive mechanism. The face is given almost nothing: a slight turn, a level gaze, no smile, no blush and no sign of the effort of standing. Read together, the two do a particular job. The picture is a marriage portrait, so it is about a position and a family, and the pattern is the family's claim rendered in fabric while the face is the sitter's contribution to it, which is to hold the position without comment. The child and the hands are part of the same economy, because they make the claim about the family concrete and stop the panel from being a display of cloth alone. Three errors to reject. There is no fixed rule that elaborate dress subordinates a sitter; here the dress and the face are set in balance, and reading one as overpowering the other describes a different panel. Nor is a cool face an unfinished one; the handling of the flesh is fully resolved, and a different key from the dress is a decision about what a face is for in a picture of this kind. The inscription belongs to the architecture in the background and is part of the setting, not a caption that overrides what is painted below it. The test: ask where the painter spent precision and where he spent nothing, and what the contrast is for.
questions.hint: Ask where the painter spent his precision and where he withheld it, and what the contrast is doing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two zones of a Toledo altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: read a split composition as a statement about where each event happens
questions.stem: A painting of 1586 to 1588 in a church in Toledo shows a funeral in a church interior at the bottom: mourners, clergy, a sarcophagus, a small angel, and at the right edge a self-portrait of the painter with his hand on a tomb. Above, the wall opens into a dark field in which the dead man's soul rises in the arms of an angel, with saints and instruments of the Passion in a cloud above. The upper figures are far longer and thinner than the lower ones. What does the change of proportion do?

options.text: It marks a stage in the work, since a painter short of time elongates the figures that are finished last
options.misconception: turns a spatial convention into evidence about the order of execution

options.text: It marks a correction, since the upper zone was repainted to make the heavens more distant from the earthly scene below
options.misconception: supplies a repainting narrative from a compositional device

options.text: It marks a change of place, so the lower zone is built of stone and the upper is dissolved, and the figures change to suit the space they are in
It marks two different painters, since a change in proportion across one canvas is the standard sign that a second hand took over
options.misconception: reads a spatial convention as evidence of a change of authorship

questions.explanation: The change of proportion is doing spatial work, and it is doing it consistently. Below, everything is built: a church interior with perspective, a sarcophagus, a crowd of identifiable mourners in ordinary proportions, a small figure of an angel at about the height of a child. Above, the field is dark and open, the figures are very much longer, and everything is lighter in tone and less firmly seated on anything. The proportion change is the convention by which this picture says heaven is a different kind of space from the church, and it is applied to the whole upper zone rather than to individual figures, which is what makes it a place rather than a manner. That is also why the lower zone includes the painter himself: the earthly register is where the people are, and one of them is the man holding the tomb. Three errors to reject, and they are all the same error in different clothes. A change of proportion across a picture is one of the most ordinary conventions in religious painting, and it is not evidence of a second hand, a hurried passage, or a repainting. What such a panel is evidence of is a painter who has decided that the distance between a church and a heaven is to be shown as a difference in how bodies stand. The test to apply: ask what each zone is made of, and whether the difference in proportion is local or systematic. Here it is systematic, and a systematic difference is a decision about place.
questions.hint: Ask whether the difference in proportion is confined to one figure or applied across a whole zone.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The objects on the shelf of a double portrait
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a group of objects as a statement rather than a list
questions.stem: A double portrait painted in 1533, oil on oak, now in the National Gallery, London, shows two richly dressed young men standing on either side of a tall narrow table. On its two shelves stand a terrestrial globe, a small book, a small image in a case, a lute, a case of flutes, a box of dice, a rosary, a small bell and a cross. What is the group of objects doing?

options.text: Balancing the composition, since a narrow table between two figures must be filled to keep the sides in equilibrium
options.misconception: makes a decorative necessity into a symbolic programme

options.text: Proving the sitters' religion, since a cross and a rosary on the same shelf fix the faith the two men practised
options.misconception: infers a personal belief from objects that may be conventional props

options.text: Enumerating possessions, since a table of objects in a portrait is the standard way of recording what a sitter owned
options.misconception: reduces a symbolic group to an inventory of property

options.text: Stating something, since the objects together name learning, music, devotion, travel and death, and the picture is about two young men whose lives combine all of them

questions.explanation: The objects are the argument, and the test of that is simple: a list would be arbitrary, and this is not. There is a globe and a cross, so travel and devotion; a lute and a case of flutes, so music, and the two together carry a well-known set of puns on the young men's names, since music and the cross are two names in Latin; a book and an image in a case, so learning; dice and a bell, so fortune and its warning; a rosary. Each object opens a subject, and each subject is something a young man of that class was expected to be involved in or to have renounced. The picture's two men are also constructed as a pair, one turned slightly towards the other across the table, so the objects are not a display in front of a wall but a statement about two lives, and the narrow table sets them at opposite sides of the same set of terms. Two errors to reject. A group of this kind is not a record of property: nothing in it is dated, nothing is local, and no inventory behaves like a well-chosen symbolic set. Nor is a symbol guaranteed to settle a private belief, since these objects circulate in court portraiture as a learned vocabulary that a sitter could accept without subscribing to every term. The fourth error is the same: a composition has to be balanced for reasons of arrangement, but the choice of what balances it is the interesting decision. Ask of each object what it opens, and if a group of them is silent on that question, it is probably inventory.
questions.hint: Ask of each object what subject it opens, and whether a list of belongings would be composed that way.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The closed exterior of the Haywain Triptych
questions.learningObjective: explain a designed exterior as a claim about a viewer
questions.stem: A triptych of about 1510, in oil on panel, made in the Low Countries and kept at a monastery near Madrid, shows on its inner faces a crowd pressing towards a hay wagon on which a group of people ride, with demons underneath and a lost panel at the left. The outer faces, when the wings are shut, carry a single traveller on a road at twilight, in a narrow strip of landscape with almost nothing in it. What does that exterior do?

options.text: It makes the outside an entry, since a solitary traveller sets the tone of a warning before the crowd and the wagon are shown at all
It protects the paint, since a closed pair of wings shields the inner panels from the light of a chapel for most of the year
options.misconception: gives a conservation function to a composition that carries a subject

options.text: It shows the panel was made for export, since a Low Countries subject in a Spanish monastery implies a market abroad
options.misconception: infers a market from a present location and a subject

options.text: It fills the space, since the frame of a triptych needs paint on its outside to match the inside and a plain board would look unfinished
options.misconception: treats a composition as a duty of matching and ignores what the traveller is for

questions.explanation: The exterior is the first thing a viewer ever sees, and this one is built as a threshold. A single figure walks alone on a road at the edge of the day, in a narrow band of landscape with almost nothing in it, and there is nothing crowded, nothing laughing and nothing coming. Read against the interior, where a crowd presses towards a hay wagon while demons move underneath it, the exterior sets the terms: a world in which everything is drawn to a single object and everything is under it. So the shut state is not the absence of a picture but the first half of a sequence, and the sequence is a warning, delivered in the register of a lonely walk before the crowd arrives. That is why the wing is so empty. A busy exterior would have given the viewer an appetite and nothing else; a nearly empty one makes the crowd on the inside feel like an event that has been sprung. Two of the distractors read a subject as a practical function. Nothing about the outer wings conserves the inner panels, and shutters in a chapel are opened and closed according to the calendar, not to keep light off paint. And the third answer confuses two kinds of fact: a panel's present location and its subject tell you something about its later history, not about the market it was made for. The fourth is a workshoper's reason that is not a reason; a frame that is visible from the street is a surface that can be painted on, and this one was. Ask what a shut altarpiece shows a passer-by, and the answer is not usually a blank board.
questions.hint: Ask what a closed triptych shows someone standing in front of it, and what that is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The barn interior of the Peasant Wedding
questions.learningObjective: explain a large interior scene built on a hanging rather than on a floor
questions.stem: A painting of 1567, oil on panel, now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, shows about a hundred and thirty people crowded into a long barn, seated on benches along a table that runs from near the front of the picture to the back wall, under a roof of rafters and hanging lamps and paper flowers and garlands. There is no perspective recession of a floor, and the crowd is arranged in horizontal bands. What is the picture's spatial device?

options.text: The absence of depth, since a crowd arranged in bands is a painter's way of admitting a scene cannot be made deep
options.misconception: treats a chosen structure as an inability to construct space

options.text: The scale of the figures, since figures of roughly one size are the only way to show a crowd of a hundred without hierarchy
options.misconception: attaches to scale a claim about hierarchy that is not made here

options.text: The hanging of objects, since the roof, the lamps and the table lines substitute for a floor and build the depth the picture needs
The roof beams, since a raftered roof is the only structure in a barn that can carry a painted ceiling convincingly
options.misconception: supplies a technical necessity where a structural convention is doing the work

questions.explanation: The barn is built from the things that hang in it, and that is the whole of the spatial idea. A long table runs from the near edge to the back wall, the rafters converge above, and between them hang lamps, paper flowers and garlands strung on cords, and these suspended objects do the work a floor and a wall would do in an interior with a vanishing point. The cords are almost the important part: they are lines at different heights and different distances, and they give the eye a ladder of planes without drawing a single tile. So the depth is real and it is constructed out of the barn's contents. The horizontal bands of figures are then the consequence of that structure rather than a substitute for it, because a crowd in a barn sits in rows, and the rows are what the long table gives the painter to organise them by. Three errors to reject. A band arrangement is a decision about how to hold a hundred people in a long thin room, and a painter who wanted a deep room with a floor could have drawn one. Nor is a raftered roof a technical requirement; it is the roof of the building the scene happens in, and it is doing symbolic as well as structural work. The fourth answer is a non sequitur: figures of similar size are not being used to deny hierarchy, they are being used because this is a table of neighbours. The test: ask which lines in the picture do the work of the floor, and count them.
questions.hint: Ask which objects in the barn are above head height, and what they are doing there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The dark foreground of a winter landscape
questions.learningObjective: explain how a dark repoussoir sets a bright distance in motion
questions.stem: A painting of 1565, oil on panel, now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, shows three hunters walking away from the viewer in the near foreground, which is very dark, with snow on their backs. Behind them the ground falls away to a village, then to frozen ponds with figures skating and sailing on them, then to a hill and a bare wood, under a pale sky. A stork stands in the snow a few feet from the hunters. What does the dark foreground do?

options.text: It sets the distance moving, since the near field is closed and unlit so that the eye is pushed out through it into the bright plain
It dates the scene, since snow with a frozen pond and skaters is a subject recorded only in the sixteenth century
options.misconception: turns a seasonal subject into a chronological index

options.text: It proves the panel was repainted, since a darkened foreground is the commonest sign of an old yellowed varnish
options.misconception: attributes a compositional device to a change in the surface

options.text: It makes the hunters the subject, since the three figures are the only large forms in a picture of small distant events
options.misconception: concludes that the subject is the figures when the composition is a journey away from them

questions.explanation: The dark foreground is a door, and a closed one. The near field is a bank of trees and brush, unlit and almost without incident, and the three hunters, seen from behind and walking out of it, are the only figures in it. That dark mass has a single function: it stops the eye at the front of the picture and gives it nothing to stay for, so the gaze is pushed out through the gap where the men are walking and into the bright plain, the village, the ponds and the wood beyond. Everything downstream of that push is then read in order, and the sequence is a descent through a landscape in full occupation. The stork a few feet from the hunters is worth pausing on, because it is the one small thing in the dark zone and it is placed there precisely so the eye catches on the way out. Three errors to reject. The hunters are the point of departure, not the subject, and a picture can be about the world beyond three people. A winter subject is not a date, since ice and skating are available to any painter of any century who chooses them. And the last is a genuine technical point misapplied: a darkened foreground here is a tonal decision, and a varnish that has yellowed uniformly is a different phenomenon, spread over the whole panel rather than concentrated in the nearest band. The test: ask what the dark zone contains, and then ask where it would have to stop for the eye to stay in it.
questions.hint: Ask what the near dark band contains, and why there is a stork in it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The magic square in an engraving
questions.learningObjective: interpret a printed diagram as evidence about a maker's interests
questions.stem: An engraving of 1514 shows a winged seated figure leaning her head on her hand on the edge of a truncated sphere, a putto sitting on a millstone beside her, an hourglass, a bell, a set of scales, a plane and a set of compasses, a dog, a set of blocks on a board, and on the wall a square of numbers arranged in four rows. What does the arrangement of those objects tell you about the print?

options.text: That the print is a puzzle for the buyer, since a square of numbers in a print can only be a problem to be solved
options.misconception: assumes every numerical device in a print is a puzzle for the reader

options.text: That the print is a satire, since a melancholy figure surrounded by instruments is a stock joke about the limits of craft
options.misconception: supplies a genre reading that ignores what the tools are shown to be

options.text: That the print was a design for a panel, since an engraving of this complexity must have been intended to be painted
options.misconception: assumes a printed design is only ever a study for another object

options.text: That the print is about the equipment of a craft, since the tools are drawn as usable objects and the numbers are a working device rather than an ornament

questions.explanation: Read the objects as a single set and the print stops being an allegory and becomes a demonstration. The scales, the plane, the compasses, the square block on a board and the set of blocks are the equipment of a skilled trade, and they are drawn with the care a craftsman gives to his own tools: at the right scale, in the right relation to the hand, resting on surfaces that make them usable. The square of numbers on the wall is a calculating device, and it is placed among them rather than apart from them, so it belongs to the same category: something that is a tool, and not a rebus. The winged figure and the putto supply the mood, and the hourglass, the bell and the dog the warnings, but the tools are the substance, and their arrangement beside the figure sets up the print's actual argument, which is about the relation between what can be measured and what cannot. Two errors to reject. A numerical device in a print of this kind is not a puzzle for the reader; a calculation is not a riddle, and treating it as one mistakes a working object for a game. And a print is a finished object, not a design for something else, however thoroughly it describes the means of another craft. The satire reading is a genre label applied to the mood while the content goes unread; the tools are what the print is about. The test: ask of each object whether it could be picked up, and the ones that could are the ones carrying the argument.
questions.hint: Ask which of the objects could be picked up, and what the numbers are for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The cosmic distance of a battle scene on panel
questions.learningObjective: account for a landscape used as a frame for a historical event
questions.stem: A panel painted in 1529, now in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich, shows two armies meeting in a plain seen from a very high viewpoint: the Turkish host in the foreground with its tents and its cannon, Alexander's line beyond, and behind them the two coasts of a strait with ships, then a town, then mountains, then clouds and a sun. A Latin inscription and four lines of verse run along the top. The armies occupy a small fraction of the picture. What is the picture's principal subject?

options.text: The topography, since the panel's value is as a record of a strait and two coasts seen from above
options.misconception: treats a landscape setting as a survey rather than as a scale device

options.text: The verse, since an inscription of this length in a painting of this kind sets out the meaning of what follows
options.misconception: gives priority to a written gloss over the spatial argument of the panel

options.text: The armies, since two hosts of many thousands are shown fighting and the fighting is what the picture is for
options.misconception: picks the human action as the subject when the composition is organised against it

options.text: The scale of the occasion, since the armies are made small in a very large landscape in order that the event can be read as part of a world

questions.explanation: The decision to make the armies small is the decision, and everything in the picture follows from it. The figures are a few hundred, the tents and cannon are tiny, and above them the ground runs through a town, hills, mountains, clouds and a sun, with the two coasts of the strait laid out to establish where the event happened. That is not a marginal: it is most of the panel. So the subject of the panel is not a battle magnified but a battle entered into the world, and the argument the picture makes is about proportion. One way of stating it: the outcome of this engagement turns on a few men crossing a river, and a picture that made the men large would have thrown that away. A second way is that the sun and the sky, so close and so bright above the plain, belong to the same order as the two commanders, which is a theological claim made purely by scale. The viewpoint, very high and tilted, is what makes the whole chain visible at once, and it is a convention with a history, derived from images of the world seen from above and not invented here. Three errors to reject. The landscape is not a survey, though the panel belongs to a tradition of topographical statement. The armies are not the subject, since the composition is organised to diminish them. And the verse is a gloss, and a gloss is not the picture's argument. Ask what would be lost if the panel were cropped to the plain, and the answer is the whole of what the painter is saying.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the panel the armies occupy, and what occupies the rest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The scale of the devouring figure in a mural of 1820
questions.learningObjective: explain how relative scale can carry a subject rather than a likeness
questions.stem: A painting of about 1819 to 1823, in oil on plaster, was made directly on the wall of a small pavilion in a garden outside Madrid, and shows a huge, naked, long-haired figure with a body the size of a building crouching over a naked child on the ground and putting the child into its mouth. The child is about a tenth of the parent's height, and both are painted at the scale the wall demands. How is scale working here?

options.text: It is the subject, since the disproportion is the point and the wall can only be filled by a monster, so nothing in the scale needs correcting
It is a residue, since the parent was first painted the same size as the child and was enlarged when the wall was found to be larger than expected
options.misconception: invents a change of scale that the composition does not require

options.text: It is a stage, since a figure this size is how a painter indicates a dream, and the dream is the picture's real subject
options.misconception: treats a scale device as a code for a kind of experience

options.text: It is a fault, since a painter would normally reduce the parent to the scale of the child and reserve the exaggeration for a print
options.misconception: supplies a scale rule from a medium the picture was not made in

questions.explanation: There is no proportional problem here, because the disproportion is the subject. The myth this picture takes is one of a parent eating its child, and the way to make that unbearable on a wall is to make the parent bigger than the room and the child the size of a body. Any other arrangement would have converted a monstrous act into a domestic one, and the child at a tenth of the parent's height is what makes the scale readable: without a known small object in the picture, a large figure means nothing. The medium is part of the answer as well, since this was painted straight onto the plaster of a garden pavilion, and a wall that size has to be given something of wall size. The brushwork is also unusually direct for a painter of this period, the handling visible and unpolished, which is what a wall of that size and a subject of that obscenity call for. Two of the distractors misread the device as an error. A general rule about relative size is not a law, and inventing one to condemn the picture contradicts its own subject, since a parent the size of a child would be a different and much less disturbing thing. A mural is not a reduced print and is not obliged to observe the conventions of one. The third answer supplies a story about the painting's making that nothing supports. The fourth is the one generalisation that is roughly right, and it is still not a correction: a scale like this is not a code a viewer has to be told about, it is the most direct way of painting what is being described. The test: ask what a person would look like at that scale against that child, and then ask whether that is the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the child at a tenth of the parent's size is there to let you judge.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The back-turned figure in the Rokeby Venus
questions.learningObjective: explain a pose chosen against the conventions of the reclining nude
questions.stem: An oil on canvas of 1650, now in the National Gallery, London, shows a reclining nude seen from behind, her back turned to the viewer, lying on a bed in a dark interior, with a man in a cloak and hat standing in silhouette at the left and a small winged figure holding a bird at the right. How is the composition arguing with the tradition of the reclining nude?

options.text: By making the figure small, since a reclining nude painted small in a large room is a way of refusing the monumental tradition
options.misconception: fixes on scale, which is the one thing this composition does not manipulate

options.text: By withholding the front, so the body is given as a mass and a back rather than as an offer, and the painting is thereby about looking at a person rather than at a body
By copying an antique relief, since a turned reclining figure was a standard subject in Roman sarcophagi
options.misconception: proposes a source that explains the pose but not the reversal of the usual presentation

options.text: By lighting the figure from behind, since a light that cannot reach the front is a deliberate refusal of the standard arrangement
options.misconception: mislocates the device, since the lighting is inside the convention rather than a reversal of it

questions.explanation: The traditional reclining nude presents itself. The body is turned so the viewer is offered a front, a breast, a face tipped back, a series of surfaces arranged to be looked at, and the whole genre is built on that offer. This picture takes the same body and turns it away, and the effect is to stop the offer in its tracks: what the viewer gets instead is a back, a hip, a shoulder blade and a curve of waist, which are surfaces that belong to a person and not to an anatomy. The composition then has to do something about the resulting vacancy, and it does it with the two flanking figures. The man in the cloak and hat is a dark, upright, almost featureless shape at one side, and the small winged figure holding a bird is a small bright one at the other, so the nude is not alone in the frame and is not simply available to the eye. The message carried by the bird and the cloak in the story is a request from a god, and the picture is about a wish granted: so the whole arrangement turns on a person being wanted rather than a body being displayed. Three errors to reject. Antique sarcophagi do have reclining figures, but a source does not explain a reversal, and the reversal is the event here. Nor is a reverse lighting a refusal of anything, since the light in this picture does what the convention expects. And scale is untouched: the figure is not unusually small, and scale is not the lever here. The lever is orientation.
questions.hint: Ask what the conventional reclining nude offers, and then ask what this one declines to offer.

questions.stem: A group portrait of 1642, oil on canvas, now in the Rijksmuseum, shows a company of about eighteen men and women in a dark interior. A man in a black coat with a red sash advances at the front left and a man in a yellow doublet with a white plume at the front right, and between and behind them a girl in a golden dress carrying a dead chicken is the most strongly lit figure in the picture, more lit than either of the two men. What does that lighting do?

options.text: It fixes the group in time, since a single strong light from one side records the hour at which the company assembled
options.misconception: reads a lighting setup as a timestamp

options.text: It shows the girl is the captain, since the strongest light in a group portrait always marks the senior figure
options.misconception: applies a rule about lighting to a group where the two officers are the principals

options.text: It makes a subsidiary figure the centre of the light, so the group's forward movement is lit from within rather than from its officers
It shows the picture was retouched, since a light area on a small figure is a typical place for a later hand to add sparkle
options.misconception: attributes a compositional highlight to a restorer

questions.explanation: The light is the argument, and it is not following rank. A company portrait is normally organised around the officers who commissioned it, and here two men are given the front, the colour and the movement: one in black and a red sash, one in yellow and a white plume, both stepping out of the group and turning outwards towards the viewer. The light, though, is on a subsidiary figure. A girl in a golden dress carrying a dead chicken is the brightest thing in the picture, and the light on her face and her sleeve comes from a source that is not the same as the light on either officer. So the picture puts its brightest value at the point where the group is most alive and least official: a child, a flash of gold, a live animal, against a row of dark coats and a background in shadow. What that does is turn a commission into a scene. The company is no longer a list of members facing a spectator; it is a body in motion with a source of energy inside it, and the light is the way the painter has said so. Three errors to reject. Light does not mark seniority; in this picture the seniors are the least lit and the most important persons, and the light is a compositional decision about interest. Nor does a light setup record an hour; an indoor scene lit from one side is a convention. And the last is a technical error applied to an expressive fact: a highlight in the middle of a picture is exactly where a painter puts one, and nothing here requires a restorer. The test: ask which figures are the principals, and then ask which are the subject.
questions.hint: Ask who the principals are, and then ask who the light picks out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The uncertain subject and the paint surface of the Jewish Bride
questions.learningObjective: separate what a surface shows from what a subject has been proposed to be
questions.stem: A painting of about 1665 to 1670, oil on canvas, now in the Rijksmuseum, shows a man placing one hand on a woman's shoulder while holding a manuscript in the other; the woman presses a hand to her chest and looks up, away from him. The paint is laid thickly, the highlights on the sleeve and the shoulder standing well above the surrounding colour. Identifications have been proposed for the couple and none has been established. Which statement is properly supported?

options.text: That the man is a rabbi and the woman his wife, since a manuscript and a hand on a shoulder are a Jewish subject by themselves
options.misconception: settles an identification from a single attribute and a gesture

options.text: That the pair are a betrothed couple, since the hand on the shoulder and the upward glance are the standard gestures of a marriage picture
options.misconception: assigns a single narrative to gestures that several readings share

options.text: That the thick paint is unfinished, since an impasto of this height is what a picture looks like before it is scraped back and finished
options.misconception: reads a deliberate heavy surface as an abandoned state

options.text: That the surface and the gesture can be described and argued about, and that the identity of the two figures is a separate and still open question

questions.explanation: Three things are being kept apart here and the question is which of them can be joined. What the surface shows is a fact: paint laid thickly, the highlights on a sleeve and a shoulder standing in relief, the colour built rather than blended, and that is a description a report can check. What the gesture shows is a fact of a different order: a hand laid on a shoulder, a hand pressed to a chest, a gaze turned upward and away, and those are observable too. What either of them means is a third thing, and it is a matter of proposal. A manuscript, a hand on a shoulder, a hand at the chest: those are the terms of a vocabulary, and they have been used for a rabbi and his wife, for a biblical pair, for a betrothed couple and for others, and no document has settled which. So the honest account is that the material and the gesture are established and the identity is open, and an answer that converts a proposal into a fact has made a category error that the evidence does not support. The impasto is worth a word because it is easy to misread. A surface built up in thick paint with the lights standing proud is a late manner that puts the drawing in the material itself, and it is a choice about touch and about the direction of the light as much as anything. The test to apply: ask of each claim whether it could be got from the object alone, from a document, or only from a comparison with pictures of other subjects.
questions.hint: Ask of the surface, the gesture and the identity which of them can be established from the object alone.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The single light and the unshown window in the Milkmaid
questions.learningObjective: account for a domestic interior organised by one light and no view
questions.stem: An interior painted about 1658 to 1660, oil on canvas, now in the Rijksmuseum, shows a maid standing at a table and pouring milk from an earthenware jug into a bowl, with a basket of bread, a bucket, a hanging lamp, a drying cloak and a door with a broken tile. There is no window in the picture. Light falls from the left across the bread, the jug and the girl's face. What is the window's absence doing?

options.text: It makes the light the event, since a single source crossing a few ordinary objects becomes the subject and the room needs no view outside it
It identifies the subject, since an unlit wall is the standard convention for a room where something secret is about to happen
options.misconception: turns a light setup into a narrative code

options.text: It shows the picture is unfinished, since a painter of this kind always set a window into the wall of a domestic interior
options.misconception: supplies a compositional habit as a test of completion

options.text: It proves the room is a cellar, since a space without a window is necessarily below ground
options.misconception: infers an architectural location from the absence of one opening

questions.explanation: The missing window is the strongest thing in the picture, and the reason is that it transfers all the work to the light. A wall with an opening in it is a demand: it asks to be looked through, and the eye leaves the room. Take the opening away and the light has nowhere to go but across the objects on the table, so the eye stays inside, on the bread, the jug, the bowl and the girl's hands and face. What that produces is a picture about attention. The light is a single, low, warm source falling from the left, and it picks out exactly three things: the broken crusts of the bread, the glazed earthenware of the jug, and the working part of the girl. Everything else, the door, the cloak, the lamp, the plaster of the wall, is in a lower key and is set there to be seen and not looked at. So the room is not a stage set and not a portrait of a person; it is an arrangement in which a woman is doing something ordinary at an ordinary moment, and the painting is about the doing. Three errors to reject. A space without a window is not necessarily underground, and the room here has a door and a lamp. Nor does the absence of a window mean the picture is unfinished; opening a wall is a decision, and a decision can be made. And an unlit wall is not a code for what is about to happen, though it has been read that way: what it is, here, is a surface to keep the light off. The test: ask where the eye leaves the picture, and notice that the answer is nowhere.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye does with a wall that has no opening in it.
