questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two pyramids and the small ship in the Raft of the Medusa
questions.learningObjective: read a compositional structure that turns on a far horizon
questions.stem: A painting of 1818 to 1819, oil on canvas, now in the Louvre, shows a raft floating on a swell. On the raft a mass of about a hundred and fifty people is built up into two sloping pyramids, the far one rising to a black man standing on a barrel and waving a cloth. The near pyramid falls away into the foreground, where a corpse lies and an old man sits holding a dead body. A mast and rigging lie broken at the right, the horizon is high, and a very small sailing ship is visible at the extreme left. What is the small ship doing?

options.text: Dating the event, since a ship of that type fixes the year in which the raft was abandoned
options.misconception: uses a vessel type as a chronological instrument it cannot provide

options.text: Giving the hope a scale, since the ship is drawn tiny and far off, so the hope it represents is a matter of a speck on the horizon
Confirming the outcome, since a rescue ship in the picture means the painter believed the survivors were saved
options.misconception: reads a painted hope as a statement of what actually happened

options.text: Balancing the composition, since a horizontal accent is needed at the left to answer the vertical of the mast on the right
options.misconception: reduces a narrative element to a compositional counterweight

questions.explanation: The ship is the measure of everything else in the picture. It is painted as a speck, near the horizon at the extreme left, while the raft fills the whole of the lower two-thirds of the canvas, and the contrast between those two sizes is the whole of the picture's information. A hundred and fifty people are crammed onto a raft, and the thing that might save them is a vessel too small to be certain about. That is why the figure at the apex is a black man standing on a barrel waving a cloth: the gesture is the largest signal the picture contains, and it is directed at a speck. The compositional design supports the same reading. Two sloping pyramids mean two states, one still arguing and one already grieving, and the foreground pair, a corpse and an old man holding a dead body, are the survivors of the argument. The high horizon keeps the sea in the top third so the raft is not surrounded by an ocean it cannot leave. Three errors to reject. A ship in the picture is a hope, not a report; a painter is not obliged to paint what happened, and the event itself ended with the survivors reaching land after days on the raft, which is not what the picture shows. Nor is the ship there to balance the mast; the balance is a consequence of where it is, and the placement at the left edge with nothing beside it is deliberate. And a vessel type is not a dating instrument: the account of what happened was published in the period, and the painting's evidence lies elsewhere. The test: ask what the ship would look like if the painter wanted the rescue to be certain, and then notice how much of the canvas would have to be given up.
questions.hint: Ask how large the ship is compared with the raft, and what that comparison tells you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The stolen berries in a printed furnishing fabric
questions.learningObjective: explain how a block-printed textile carries an argument about nature and trade
questions.stem: A furnishing fabric of 1883, block printed in colour on a plain ground by a firm of designers and makers working for the middle-class reform market, shows a close view of a meadow with three thrushes stooping at a clump of strawberries, the birds drawn with a sharpness that has nothing to do with natural observation and the berries enlarged well beyond life size. The design was adapted from a published wood engraving. What is the fabric doing with its source?

options.text: Rejecting it, since a design for a printed page is a commercial image and a design for cloth is a moral statement about what a room should contain
options.misconception: sets up a moral opposition between two media that the design does not exploit

options.text: Copying it, since a printed design transferred to cloth is by definition a reproduction of the engraving it came from
options.misconception: confuses using a source with reproducing it

options.text: Converting it, since an image made to be looked at closely is rebuilt as a repeat that can be hung in a room, and the scale is changed to suit cloth
Dating it, since the presence of a published engraving as a source places the design in the year the engraving appeared
options.misconception: uses a source's date as the design's date

questions.explanation: A repeat is a different object from a single image, and the conversion is the designer's actual work. An engraving is looked at once, at a distance, framed, on a page; a furnishing fabric is looked at continuously, from across a room, and it has to tile. So the image is rebuilt: the field is regularised, the motif is scaled to a repeat unit, the outlines are strengthened so they survive printing and washing, and the colour is reduced to a small working number of blocks. The enlargement of the strawberries is a consequence of that, because on cloth a motif has to read across a room and the fruit is what carries the recognisable idea. The sharpness of the thrushes is the other half of the conversion, since a printed repeat cannot afford the irregularity of a drawn bird and the shapes are built as pattern. So the source is a proposal and the fabric is the answer. Three errors to reject. Using a published image is not the same as reproducing it, and the whole of the designer's contribution lies in what changed. Nor is there a moral opposition between a page and a cloth; a drawing made for reproduction is available to whoever can buy it, and the sharp observation of the birds is a claim about attention, not a commercial failure. And a source's date is not a design's date, since a designer can work from an old print for years. The test: ask what would have to change to make the image tile, and then look at what did change.
questions.hint: Ask how a repeat differs from a framed image, and what the enlargement is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The missing painting and the second version of the Stone Breakers
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an official record of loss from a contested account of how a work was lost
questions.stem: A painting of 1849, oil on canvas about one and a half metres high and two and a half metres wide, was shown at the Paris Salon of 1850 and later entered a collection in Dresden. It has long been described as destroyed when a vehicle carrying evacuated pictures was hit during the bombing of Dresden in February 1945, but the Dresden institution records the picture as missing rather than destroyed, and a second version of the subject, with the image reversed, is held in a collection in Winterthur. Which of these facts can be used, and how?

options.text: None of it can be used, since a picture recorded as missing cannot support any argument about the work or about the movement it belongs to
options.misconception: concludes that a record of loss removes a work from the evidence

options.text: Only the account of the bombing, since a documented loss is the firmest kind of evidence a lost work can produce
options.misconception: treats a story of a loss as a document

options.text: Only the reversal, since a mirrored version is a copy and therefore tells us nothing about how the first was painted
options.misconception: asserts that a reversed version carries no information at all

options.text: The reversal and the record of loss can both be used, while the account of how it was lost has to be argued from documents, because the two claims answer different questions

questions.explanation: The three facts have to be used at their own strength, and the interesting one is the third. A reversed second version is not a copy in the sense that would make it useless: it is the same subject painted again, and being a mirror image of the first it has to have been made from a model rather than from the original, which means the original was available to be modelled from. So the second version is direct evidence that the Salon picture existed, was seen, and was worth remaking, and it is also a document about the priority of the two. That is a real contribution and it does not depend on knowing how the first was lost. The loss itself is a separate matter and the record is carefully worded: an institution that says missing is not saying destroyed, and the difference is not pedantry. It is the difference between a claim with a cause attached and a claim that something was not accounted for. Whether the picture was on a convoy, whether it was transferred in 1944, and whether the fire account is a later simplification are all questions for documents, and the answer to that question does not change the other two facts. Three errors to reject. A record of loss does not remove a work from the evidence; on the contrary, the loss and the versions are what make this one of the most cited cases in the history of nineteenth-century painting. A mirrored version is not information-free. And an account of a loss, however often repeated, is not a document; a document is the piece of paper that would settle it, and nobody has produced one. The test: ask which of the three claims could survive if the bombing story turned out to be wrong.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three facts would still be true if the bombing story were wrong.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The divided touch of a figure on the island in La Grande Jatte
questions.learningObjective: account for a shadow and a touch technique working together
questions.stem: A painting begun in 1884 and worked on until 1886, oil on canvas, now in the Art Institute of Chicago, shows about a hundred and twenty people on an island in a river on a bright afternoon. The surface is built from small separate touches of unmixed colour, and the shadows on the grass are laid in as small touches of contrasting colour rather than as mixed grey. What is the double effect of those two choices?

options.text: The shadows become colour and the light becomes grain, so the light is in the material of the surface and the picture is at once flat and full of air
Both are effects of underpainting, since divided colour and a coloured shadow are what appear when a warm ground is left showing through
options.misconception: attributes both visible results to a ground rather than to the surface handling

options.text: The surface is correct and the shadows are wrong, since a shadow on grass at midday is brown and not blue
options.misconception: supplies a fixed local colour for a shadow and ignores its function

options.text: The shadows are correct and the surface is a limitation, since a picture built from dots can only be decorative and cannot represent depth
options.misconception: concludes that a divided touch rules out depth when the depth here is stated by another means

questions.explanation: Two decisions are being made at once and they are of opposite kinds. The first is chromatic: the shadows on the grass are not mixed greys and browns but touches of the colours opposite them, blue-violet against yellow, which is a method that depends on the eye mixing at a distance and on the picture being seen in daylight. The consequence is that shadow stops being a lack of light and becomes a presence of a different colour, so the sunlit grass and the shadowed grass are equally material and equally coloured. The second is structural: the whole surface is built from small separate touches of unmixed colour, so there is no blended transition anywhere and the image is made of a grain. Together the two do something that neither does alone. The figures are held apart and flattened, because the touches are discrete and the space between them is never fused, and yet the air is palpable, because a low sun through leaves and a wind on the water are the things the grain most easily conveys. That is a flat picture with air in it, which is the hard thing to do. Three errors to reject. A divided touch does not prevent depth: the depth here is stated by scale, by overlap and by the arrangement of the figures on the bank, and it is stated perfectly well. Nor is a shadow a fixed local colour; a colour used to make a shadow is judged by what it does against what surrounds it, and at midday under a bright sky a blue shadow is a better shadow than a brown one. The last answer misattributes both results to an underpainting: nothing here depends on a warm ground, and the shadows are opaque touches laid on top, not the ground showing through.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye is asked to do at the distance you normally view a picture from.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A figure designed for a doorway and later exhibited alone
questions.learningObjective: trace how a component becomes an independent work
questions.stem: A bronze nude of a seated man leaning forward with his chin on the back of his right hand was modelled about 1880 to 1881 as part of a monumental doorway of about six metres high, where the figure sat above the entrance. It was exhibited on its own in 1889, and a much larger version was worked between 1902 and 1904, from which the first of the familiar monumental bronze casts was made in 1904. What does that sequence establish?

options.text: That the doorway was never made, since a figure that has been exhibited alone has left its original setting
options.misconception: concludes from a later career that a setting never existed

options.text: That the first version is a study, since anything modelled small and later enlarged must have been a preliminary design
options.misconception: supposes a fixed relation between scale and status that the two dates contradict

options.text: That the figure has two histories, since its meaning as a component of a scheme and its meaning as a free-standing work were made at different times by different decisions
That the seated pose is classical, since a naked seated man in a thinking position is a figure from a Greek sculpture and the pose is therefore a quotation
options.misconception: assigns a single classical source to a pose with several known precedents

questions.explanation: The dates are the whole of the answer, and they should be read as two sequences rather than one. Between about 1880 and 1881 the figure was a component: a seated body on the tympanum of a doorway, part of a scheme about a poem, one figure among many, and its job was to hold a place in an architecture and to be read at the scale of the whole. In 1889 it was exhibited alone, and at that moment a second question was put to it, which is what a work is when nothing frames it and nothing accompanies it. Then the enlargement between 1902 and 1904 and the first monumental cast in 1904 produced a third object, a life-size-plus version conceived for its own sake, and it is that one which became the version everyone knows. So the figure has at least three identities and they were produced by decisions, not by accident of scale. Three errors to reject. A small version that is later enlarged is not a study; a component is finished for its place, and the two dates here are twenty years apart. Nor does exhibiting a figure alone show the setting never existed; the doorway was made, and the sequence of the record is not the sequence of the object. And the pose has more than one antecedent, among them a painted and a carved group of about the 1860s, so a single classical source is not available and the pose was arrived at rather than quoted. The test: for any object with a documented enlargement or a documented extraction, ask what the object was for before the date and what it was for after it.
questions.hint: Ask what the figure was for in 1881 and what it was for in 1889, and whether those are the same job.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three arches and the divided family in the Oath of the Horatii
questions.learningObjective: read a picture organised by an architecture that divides its figures
questions.stem: A painting of 1784, oil on canvas, now in the Louvre, shows three men on the left, all in Roman dress, each standing rigidly with one arm extended towards three swords held horizontally in the middle by an old man. On the right are women and children, curved and grouped, one of them collapsed against a seat. The three men are each framed in one of three identical round arches; the women's group is under a darker vault set at an angle. What is the architecture doing?

options.text: Ranking, since a man under his own arch outranks a man sharing one, and the three arches are three degrees of virtue
options.misconception: reads an architectural partition as a graded scale of virtue

options.text: Quoting, since three arches in a row is a convention taken from a Roman triumphal relief and the picture is a restatement of it
options.misconception: proposes a derivation where a partitioning function is available

options.text: Partitioning, since the three arches hold the three men apart from each other and the angled vault holds the women apart from them
Receding, since a set of round arches drawn side by side is the only device that can show a wall going away from the viewer
options.misconception: claims a spatial function for a scheme that separates rather than recedes

questions.explanation: The architecture is a partition, and the partition is the moral argument of the picture. Three identical round arches, side by side, each with a man in it, hold the three brothers apart: they are of one mind and they are not together. Their arms all go the same way, towards the same three swords held out in the middle by their father, and the line of those arms plus the horizontal of the blades is the only line in the picture that crosses between them. On the other side, the women's group is put under a vault that is darker and set at an angle, so it does not share the men's architecture at all, and within it the figures are curved, collapsed and interlocked, with one woman turned away entirely. So the picture's whole argument is made of two kinds of space: three straight, separate, identical compartments and one dark oblique one that holds everybody who is connected to the other family. That is a formal statement about a moral choice, and it is made before any of the costumes are read. Three errors to reject. A man under his own arch is not thereby higher than his brothers; the three are equal and the arches are what make them equal. Nor are three arches a device for recession; they are side by side on a single plane, and a receding arcade would show the near arch larger. And a possible Roman precedent does not explain a partition, whereas a partitioning function explains the exact number, the exact symmetry and the exact place of the swords. The test: ask which figures share a compartment and which do not, and what the sharing implies.
questions.hint: Ask which figures share a compartment, and where the only line that crosses between them is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The empty room and the light in the Death of Marat
questions.learningObjective: account for a picture whose setting is given almost entirely by light
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting of 1793, oil on canvas, now in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts, Brussels, shows a young man who has been killed in his bath, lying with his head back and one arm hanging over the side of a wooden bath, which is covered by a coarse cloth used as a desk. A letter and a quill lie on the cloth, a dark stain runs from a wound in the chest, and a plain wooden brush handle protrudes from the hand that held it. The room is almost empty, with a plain wall behind, a cloth hanging at the left, and light falling from above and slightly in front. What is the light doing?

options.text: Establishing a presence, since the light falls on a face and a wound as if on a body laid out, and everything else in the room is only what is needed to say what happened
Hiding the room, since a painter who wants the viewer to look at the face will always keep the setting as plain as possible
options.misconception: turns a deliberate reduction of setting into a general rule about looking

options.text: Separating the victim from the assassin, since the light falls on the body and not on anything that could belong to the man who attacked him
options.misconception: looks for a second person in a room the description shows to be empty

options.text: Recording the time of day, since a light from above and in front can only come from a window at a fixed hour
options.misconception: reads a lighting scheme as a timestamp

questions.explanation: The light in this picture behaves like a laying-out. It falls from above and slightly in front, it takes the face, the chest and the wound, and it leaves almost everything else in a half-tone, so the room appears not as a room but as a setting prepared for a body. That is why so much of the description is inventory of a few plain things: a coarse cloth thrown over the bath, a letter, a quill, a plain wall, a hanging cloth, a brush handle. Each one is there because it says something, and none of them is there to be a room. The wooden brush handle is the sharpest of them, since a sophisticated implement reduced to a stick says that the man was working, and the fact that his hand still holds it says he was interrupted. The stain running from the wound does the rest, and it is allowed to run downward across the cloth because the picture is about a life stopping, not about a wound being examined. Three errors to reject. A light from a direction is a convention, not a clock, and painters of this period used high frontal light for any subject that had to be legible. Nor is a plain setting a general rule; it is a decision with consequences, because an empty room is a claim that the man died alone. And there is no second person in the room: nothing in the description belongs to an assassin, and the light is not excluding a figure that is not there. The test: ask what each object in the picture is doing, and the ones that do nothing will not survive the question.
questions.hint: Ask which objects in the room are there to say something, and which are there to be a room.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The elongation of a reclining figure in the Grande Odalisque
questions.learningObjective: account for a distortion that is a decision rather than an error
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting dated 1814, oil on canvas, now in the Louvre, shows a reclining nude seen from behind and above, the back and hips turned towards the viewer and the head turned away and small. The proportions are lengthened: the torso is very long, the hip high, the upper arm short. The flesh is modelled in a smooth enamel-like finish with almost no cast shadow, the colours are cool and even, and behind her a small seated figure, a guitar, a round table with a book of music and a shawl complete the room. What is the lengthening for?

options.text: Nothing, since a lengthening of this kind is a documented failure of drawing that the painter's own circle took him to task for
options.misconception: assumes a corrective motive from a community that also defended the distortion

options.text: Hiding the anatomy, so a body drawn with wrong proportions cannot be compared with a correct one and the viewer's judgement is prevented
options.misconception: ascribes to the distortion a purpose that concerns the viewer's perception

options.text: Making the room large, since a long body inside a small room is the standard way of suggesting that the space extends beyond the frame
options.misconception: mislocates the effect, since the distortion is in the body rather than in the space

options.text: Controlling the roll, so the back can be turned towards the viewer and unrolled at the waist, which a correct proportion would not permit

questions.explanation: The lengthening is a solution to a pose. The back is turned towards the viewer, the head away, the hip raised, the upper arm brought down in front, and a body of correct proportions simply will not do that: turn a torso hard enough for the back to face you and the waist disappears. A painter who wanted that roll of flesh to run as an unbroken line from shoulder to hip had to lengthen the section between them, and the lengthening is placed exactly where the pose requires it and nowhere else. So the distortion is local and purposeful. The surface treatment belongs to the same kind of decision. A smooth, near-shadowless finish in cool, even colours refuses the warm, soft, shadowed flesh of a tradition this painter spent his career arguing against, and it is a refusal of a style rather than an inability to model: there is plenty of modelling, there is simply very little cast shadow and no warm flesh. Three errors to reject. A distortion on a canvas like this was defended, not only attacked, by the people around it, so a corrective motive needs evidence and there is none. And the effect is not to enlarge a room; the room behind is small and the point is that the body has been made to fit a pose. The last answer is incoherent: nothing here is about preventing judgement, since the whole picture is an argument with a public that could see exactly what had been done. The test to apply: ask what the body is trying to do, and then ask which part of its length makes that possible.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the body is extended, and what the pose would be impossible without that extension.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The pyramid of a figure holding a flag
questions.learningObjective: explain how a crowd is built into a single figure in a history painting
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting of 1830, oil on canvas, now in the Louvre, shows a crowd filling the lower two-thirds of the picture. At the centre and rising above all of them is a bare-breasted woman who steps forward holding a flag in her right hand and a bayonet in her left. Around her: a boy climbing over a barricade with a pair of pistols, a man in a top hat and a frock coat holding a musket, kneeling and fallen figures, and a man in a workman's cap and shirt raising a knife. At the right, through the smoke, a tower. What is the arrangement of the figures doing?

options.text: Distributing the weapons, since a musket, a pair of pistols, a bayonet and a knife are shown so the viewer can count the arms of the insurrection
options.misconception: reads an inventory of weapons as the picture's subject

options.text: Inventing a woman, since a bare breast in a crowd of men is a convention that no crowd in a real city would have produced
options.misconception: treats an allegorical figure as a report of what was present

options.text: Making one argument, since the people who are looking are put into the bodies of those who are looking, and the whole crowd is lifted into a single figure
Crowding the frame, since a painting of this size needed a hundred figures and the painter filled the space because it was available
options.misconception: explains a composition by the size of the canvas

questions.explanation: The structure is a pyramid and its point is a woman, and the reason the crowd works is that the people in it are shown looking. Almost every figure is directed: the boy with the pistols goes forward and up, the man with the musket goes forward, the man with the knife comes up through the middle, and the kneeling and fallen bodies are placed along the two slopes of the triangle. The effect is that the whole crowd is carried up into the woman, so that what the viewer sees is not a mob plus a flag-bearer but a single mass with a summit. And the summit is a figure who is not in the crowd at all: bare-breasted, barefoot, classical in her drapery, holding a light in one hand and a blade in the other, in the visual language of a figure of Liberty. So the painting's claim is a compositional claim: the mixed crowd of a city in revolt is unified by an idea, and the picture shows the unification by putting the idea at the top of the mass. Three errors to reject. A bare breast in a revolutionary picture is a figure of an idea and not a report of a person, so nothing is invented about the crowd. The weapons are not an inventory; they are what identifies each body's part in the action, and they are varied so that the slopes are legible. And a crowd is not placed to fill a canvas, it is placed to build a shape, and the shape here is the argument. The test: ask what the eye is carried up to, and then ask whether that thing is in the crowd or above it.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye is carried up to, and whether that thing belongs to the crowd.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The lantern on the ground in the Third of May
questions.learningObjective: explain a single object that reverses the relation of light between two groups
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting of 1814, oil on canvas, now in the Museo del Prado, shows a firing squad of soldiers at the left, seen from behind and largely in shadow, one of them with his rifle raised. Facing them at the right is a row of about six men in white shirts with their arms above their heads, illuminated strongly, and one of them has been struck and is falling. On the ground between the two groups is a square lantern, and behind the row of men the land falls away to a low horizon in haze. What does the lantern do?

options.text: It fixes the time, since a lantern lit on open ground establishes that the event happened after dark
options.misconception: treats a lighting device as a timestamp when the scene is plainly in daylight

options.text: It proves the picture is a copy, since a square lantern of this kind appears in several earlier treatments of the same event
options.misconception: invents a copy relation from a repeated motif

options.text: It reverses the lighting, since the lantern that has been put down to give the squad its light now lights the victims, and the men are the brighter party
It explains the execution, since a lantern left on the ground shows that the squad was improvising rather than following orders
options.misconception: infers a state of mind from an object that the picture uses compositionally

questions.explanation: The lantern is the hinge of the whole picture, and its power is that it hands the light over. A firing squad at night or in the dark would carry a lantern to see its target, and that lantern would be at the soldiers' feet and behind their line. Here it is on the ground between the two groups, and the illumination has passed across: the men in white shirts are the brightest thing in the picture, brightly and flatly lit, while the soldiers at the left are dark, turned away, and seen mostly as silhouette. So the light is on the victims, and the machinery of the killing is in the dark. The composition makes the same point geometrically. The squad is a compact dark mass on the left with a single horizontal line of heads; the row of men is a bright vertical-and-horizontal armature of arms, at the right, and the two groups face each other across a small illuminated floor. Behind the row of men the land falls away into a low hazy horizon, so they are not backed by anything: they stand against a distance, and the soldier is backed by the mass of his own firing line. The arms above the heads make a shape that is nearly a cross, which is a reading available rather than a stated one. Three errors to reject. A lantern is a device, not a clock, and this scene is plainly in daylight. Nor does a lantern on the ground show that anything was improvised. And a motif recurring in earlier treatments of an event is evidence about how painters handled the event, not about a copy.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two groups the light is on, and what a lantern is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The horse's head through a curtain in the Nightmare
questions.learningObjective: account for a figure that does not belong to the room it enters
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting dated 1781, oil on canvas, now in the Detroit Institute of Arts, shows a woman asleep on a bed, her arm hanging down and her head fallen back, in a room with a curtain across the top. Through a gap in the curtain a large white horse's head pushes in, wide-eyed and with the nostril flared. On the woman's chest crouches a small figure with a hard, jointed body and pointed features, and a lamp glows on a table at the left. A second painting on the reverse of the same canvas shows a shepherd asleep while the same small figure sits on him, with the horse behind. What is the arrangement doing?

options.text: Placing two bodies where one should be, so the pressure is doubled and the small figure is felt to be on the sleeper and on the viewer at once
Illustrating a belief, since a horse's head at a window is a documented emblem of a particular disease and the picture is an illustration of it
options.misconception: reduces the composition to a single emblematic lookup

options.text: Copying a print, since the reversed image is a documented result of working without a mirror, which settles the question of how it was made
options.misconception: accepts a story about the reversal as a complete account of the picture

options.text: Drawing on a stage, since the curtain across the top shows the scene is a play and the horse is a property
options.misconception: reads a framing device as evidence of a theatrical source

questions.explanation: The composition is a device for putting a body where a body is not expected, and it works by doubling. A woman asleep on a bed has one thing on her chest, and the small jointed figure supplies it. The horse's head then comes through a curtain in a room that has no door, and it is very large in relation to the bed, so the second presence is larger and less explicable than the first. The result is a picture in which the sleeper is being pressed from below and observed from outside the wall at the same time, and the small figure is doing both jobs at once: it is a thing that sits on the chest of whoever is asleep, and the viewer is asleep to a scene. The second canvas on the reverse confirms the structure, because there the figure sits on a shepherd and the horse is again behind, so the pairing of a large animal and a small intruder is the subject and not an accident of one night. The lamp at the left, low and guttering, is what allows the room to be seen at all and does no narrative work. Three errors to reject. A curtain across the top is a framing device common in pictures of this kind and is not evidence of a stage. The horse's head is not reducible to a single emblem lookup, and an illustration would not build a doubled structure. And the story about working without a mirror is a claim about how an artist made an image, offered in a particular way; it settles nothing about the composition and it is not needed to understand it. The test: ask what the small figure would be doing if the horse were not there.
questions.hint: Ask what the small figure is doing on the chest, and what the horse is doing to the same room.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A small sun and a large sky in a harbour scene
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the naming of a picture against what the picture does
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting dated 1872, oil on canvas, now in the Musee Marmottan Monet in Paris, shows a harbour mouth in a haze. Two small rowing boats with dark hulls and pale sails sit in the middle distance, a third larger boat with a funnel and two masts is at the right, and a crowd of small figures stands on a jetty at the left. Above the horizon the sky fills two-thirds of the canvas, and the sun is a disc of orange and pale yellow sitting in it with a reflected glitter of the same colours running down the water. The name the picture is now known by was given to it in a newspaper review published two years after it was painted. What does that naming tell you?

options.text: That the picture is about the sun, since a title is normally chosen by the painter and painters name their subjects accurately
options.misconception: assumes a title records an intention without evidence

options.text: That the picture has no subject, since a work that has been renamed can have no consistent account of what it is about
options.misconception: concludes that a later name removes the possibility of description

options.text: That the picture was painted for a review, since a reviewer cannot coin a name for a picture nobody had asked him about
options.misconception: reverses the relation between a picture and a review of it

options.text: That the name is evidence about a reception, and it needs to be tested against the picture, since the sun is a device here rather than the subject the title proposes

questions.explanation: A title is a piece of reception history, and this one is a good case because the name and the picture are about different things. The picture is a harbour: two-thirds sky, a low horizon, a glitter path of broken colour running down the water from a small disc, dark hulls and pale sails in the haze, and a jetty. The sun is a device, and it is doing a job that has nothing to do with being the subject. It is the source of the reflected glitter that breaks the water into a field of separate strokes, which is the point of the exercise, and it is the only place where warm colour is allowed into a canvas otherwise built from cool greys and pale blues. So the picture's account is about the effect of a light source on a surface, and the picture's name, coined in a hostile review, is about a set of brushmarks. Both can be true at once, and the method is to ask what the title is evidence of. A title applied in a review is evidence of how a critic characterised a group of pictures; it is not evidence of the painter's intention, and the common claim that the painter made the picture to supply a word to a reviewer is a later construction that no document supports. Three errors to reject. Titles are not chosen accurately by definition, and a critical coinage certainly was not. A review postdates the picture it reviews. And a name has no power to deprive a work of a describable subject, which the description above has just done. The test: when a title and a picture disagree, say what kind of document each is.
questions.hint: Ask what a title coined in a review is evidence of, and what the sun is doing in the picture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The cypress and the village in a night landscape
questions.learningObjective: account for a composition that turns on two contradictory demands
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting of 1889, oil on canvas, now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York, shows a night sky filling about two-thirds of the canvas, with a great swirl of light in the upper left, a bright disc with a halo above the horizon at the right, and eleven stars set in the swirl, each with a halo of light. Below, a village with a single church spire sits in the middle distance, and in the left foreground a dark cypress rises almost the full height of the picture, its flame-like brushwork turning. What does the cypress do?

options.text: Fixing the season, since a cypress is a Mediterranean tree and its presence identifies the place of the scene
options.misconception: uses a tree species as a geographical instrument it cannot reliably provide

options.text: Blocking the view, since a tree of that height standing in the foreground must obstruct whatever is behind it
options.misconception: describes the tree's extent without asking what its function is

options.text: Joining the two halves, since its dark mass rises from the village to the sky and is worked in the same loaded stroke that carries the swirl, so earth and air are made of one material
Proving the picture was painted from memory, since a view of this complexity cannot be assembled without an invention of that kind
options.misconception: infers working conditions from the complexity of a composition

questions.explanation: The cypress is the join, and the reason is that it is the only object in the picture that is made of the same stuff as the sky. It stands in the near foreground on the left and rises almost the full height of the canvas, and it is worked in thick, directional, flame-like strokes that turn the trunk into a vertical of the same energy as the swirl above. A tree that is at once earth and air is what allows the picture to keep going: the village is quiet, small and cool, with one spire, and the sky is loud, and the cypress carries the loudness down into the ground so the two halves belong to one world rather than two. The impulse behind that is a real problem. The surface of a night sky in paint tends to go dead and grey, and the way out is not to smooth it but to build it, so the stars and the swirl are made of loaded, directional strokes that hold light. The dark blues and greens of the canvas are doing the same job elsewhere, keeping the whole surface saturated so the lights have something to be brighter than. Three errors to reject. A tree in a foreground does not have to obstruct; a dark vertical mass placed at the edge of a composition is one of the standard ways of holding a picture's side open. Nor does a tree species locate a scene by itself. And the last is an inference from nothing: a picture can be worked up over months in a room from a memory or from an earlier drawing, and the complexity of a canvas is not evidence of either. The test: ask which part of the picture the foreground is connected to.
questions.hint: Ask what the cypress is made of, and what the same brushwork is doing in the sky.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The tilted table in a still life
questions.learningObjective: explain an inconsistent perspective used deliberately
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting of about 1890 to 1893, oil on canvas, now in the Art Institute of Chicago, shows a table seen from slightly above, tipped up towards the viewer so that its front edge runs across the picture and everything on it is presented almost from above. On the table are a green bottle, a wine glass tipped so that its stem points at the viewer, two cups of different sets, one striped and one plain, with their saucers, a heap of fruit, and a folded cloth. Behind, a second table at an angle, a hanging patterned cloth, a chair and a wall. The picture does not add up to one consistent set of vanishing points. What is the inconsistency for?

options.text: Signalling a dream, since a picture that cannot be spatially consistent is the standard way of showing that nothing in it is real
options.misconception: treats an inconsistent scheme as a code for unreality

options.text: Letting each thing be seen, since a table tilted towards the viewer shows the whole of what is on it, and a common viewpoint would hide half the arrangement
Copying a source, since a set of cups of two patterns in one picture is a sign that the painter worked from another picture
options.misconception: reads a familiar still-life arrangement as evidence of a copy

options.text: Compensating for the room, since a low viewpoint can be made consistent by tilting the objects that do not fit the scheme
options.misconception: describes a compensation but mistakes the inconsistency for a system

questions.explanation: The tilted table is a viewing decision, and it can be checked by asking what a consistent scheme would have hidden. Set the table flat at eye level and the fruit is seen from the side, the cups are cut in half by the table edge, the saucers disappear behind the objects standing on them, and the front of the cloth is not visible. Tilt the whole arrangement up towards the viewer and every object presents its face at once: the top of the heap of fruit, the rim of the jar, the interior of the cup, the surface of the folded cloth. The same reasoning governs the glass, whose stem is pushed towards the viewer so that the bowl and the liquid inside are legible, and the two cups, which are not a matched set and are there partly to be seen as two different objects rather than as a pair. And the inconsistency is deliberate, not an error: each object is tilted according to what it has to show, so the picture's coherence is thematic rather than optical, holding together by a shared angle of attention rather than by a shared vanishing point. The back of the room, with its second table at a different angle and its patterned hanging, is set in a scheme that does not agree with the front, and that disagreement is part of the argument. Three errors to reject. Two sets of cups is a convention of this kind of still life, not evidence of a copy. A compensation is a correction that makes a scheme consistent, and there is no consistency here to compensate. And an inconsistent scheme is not a code for unreality; it is what happens when a painter chooses to see several things at once. The test: name a single object and ask what viewpoint would have hidden it.
questions.hint: Ask what a consistent eye-level table would have hidden from you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The figures cut by the edge of a rainy street
questions.learningObjective: explain cropping as a decision about where a picture begins
questions.stem: The following description is written for this question. A painting of 1877, oil on canvas, now in the Musee d'Orsay, shows a wide street of uniform apartment buildings under a grey sky, the wet asphalt taking reflections of the buildings, the sky and the figures. A woman with a black umbrella crosses close to the picture plane at the left, and behind her two men are cut in half by the frame, one of them cut at the middle of the body and the other at the shoulder, and at the right edge a man in a top hat is cut by a lamp post. Nobody is looking at anything, and there is no central event. What does the cropping do?

options.text: Saving space, since a canvas of that size could not hold a full-length figure for every passer-by
options.misconception: explains a compositional decision by an economy of space

options.text: Fixing a place, since bodies cut at the edge say that this street continues past the picture in both directions and is not a stage set
Copying a photograph, since a cropped figure at the edge of a frame is the signature of a camera
options.misconception: infers a photographic source from a convention shared with photography

options.text: Blurring the subject, since a figure cut in half is by definition a figure whose identity the picture refuses
options.misconception: treats a crop as a statement about identity rather than about extent

questions.explanation: A crop at the edge is a claim about extent. A figure cut in half at the frame says that the body continues, and that the street, the pavement and the crowd continue, and that the picture has taken a slice of something larger rather than composed a self-contained arrangement of whole people. This is what stops the street from being a stage. Every figure here is at some stage of crossing and none of them is going anywhere in particular, and the two men behind the umbrella are not the principal subjects; they are the crowd the woman is walking through. The buildings carry the same message at the other edges, since the rows of uniform facades run out of the picture at both ends and the perspective lines of the cornices and the kerb do not converge inside the frame. So the picture is about a place rather than an event, and the cropping is the device that makes the place real: a thing that ends at the frame is a thing that has been arranged. Three errors to reject. Space is not a motive, since a wide canvas takes as many figures as the painter puts on it. And a cropped figure is not a figure whose identity is refused; an anonymous passer-by is anonymous in a full-length figure too, and a crop has nothing to say about who a person is. The last is a real question asked wrongly: photographs crop like this, and painters have cropped like this for a long time, so the convention does not decide the medium. The test: ask what is implied to be just outside the frame, and whether the picture wants that implication.
questions.hint: Ask what the cut figures imply is happening just outside the frame.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A block and pigment report on a printed wave
questions.learningObjective: read a technical report on a print as evidence about how a colour is obtained
questions.stem: A report on a colour woodblock print of about 1831 reads: the design is an oban sheet in horizontal format, from a series of thirty-six views of a mountain; it was printed from a key block with a small number of further blocks, three of them for the three shades of blue in the water, one for the yellow of the boat sides, one for the low sky, one pale grey, and a pinkish one barely visible; the strongest blue is a synthetic pigment that had recently become cheaply available from China and does not fade; the outlines of early impressions are blue, and impressions printed after the series was extended carry black outlines instead. What has the report established?

options.text: That a synthetic pigment and a division of labour determined the look, and that the outline colour records two stages in the series' issue
That the print is a copy of a painting, since a work using a newly available imported pigment cannot be original to the tradition of Japanese painting
options.misconception: infers dependence from the arrival of a pigment

options.text: That the print was made in a single impression, since a report listing several blocks describes one sheet printed in one go
options.misconception: confuses the blocks used with the number of impressions pulled

options.text: That the mountain is a portrait of a particular place, since a series of thirty-six views of one peak is a survey of that peak
options.misconception: treats a series title as a topographical record

questions.explanation: A report like this is a description of a division of labour, and there are two things in it. The first is that the strongest blue is a synthetic pigment recently imported and available in quantity, which is a fact about trade and cost as much as about colour, and it explains why the water can carry three distinguishable blues at all. Before a cheap non-fading blue was available, a printer needing several blues either had to mix them from what he had or accept one. So the number of blues in the design is a consequence of a supply change, which is a real and datable fact about the medium in that decade. The second is the outline. Blue outlines on the earlier issues and black outlines on the later ones, following the extension of the series, are the trace of a decision taken by the publisher to add ten more views and change the outlines at the same time, so the outline colour is a stage marker and a piece of publishing history visible on the sheet. Two of the distractors confuse levels. Several blocks means several colours, not a single impression; a print run of thousands is what these blocks were cut for. And the arrival of a pigment is a change in what was available, not evidence that a painter was imitating a foreign picture. The last reads a series title as a survey: thirty-six views of one mountain is a set of invented viewpoints, not a record of a place. The test: ask of each line of the report whether it is about the making, the issue, or the subject.
questions.hint: Ask of each line of the report whether it is about the making, the issue, or the subject.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A darkened campaign revealed on an oil canvas
questions.learningObjective: read a treatment report as evidence about a picture's original state
questions.stem: A painting of the 1570s, oil on canvas, suffered severe damage at some point after it was made, and a report records that the upper part of the canvas carried a darkened, discoloured layer; that examination under the raking light and in ultraviolet showed the layer to be a later campaign and not part of the original paint; and that removing it revealed a bright sky and the raised, outstretched hand of the central figure, which the darkened layer had almost concealed. What does the report establish?

options.text: That the picture was never finished, since an unaltered passage appearing under a darkened one implies that the work was left incomplete
options.misconception: treats a hidden passage as evidence of an unfinished state

options.text: That the hand is a later addition, since a raised figure standing out from a flat sky must have been repainted to be seen
options.misconception: infers a later hand from the contrast between a passage and its surroundings

options.text: That the painter repainted his own sky, since a later campaign on a canvas is most simply the artist returning to it
options.misconception: assigns a later campaign to the painter without any evidence of who applied it

options.text: That the picture was altered after it was finished, and that the alteration concealed a passage of the original composition, so the recovered state is earlier than anything a photograph since the damage can show

questions.explanation: The chain of reasoning in the report is a good model, and it is worth following in order. A darkened area is noticed; examination distinguishes a later layer from original paint; the layer is removed; and what is under it is recorded. The conclusion is therefore about sequence, not about authorship. The darkened layer was applied after the picture was finished, and it was covering a passage of the composition, so the state now visible is earlier than the state that any photograph taken since the damage would show. That has a consequence for evidence. A photograph of a damaged picture is a document of the damage, and anyone arguing about the original composition has to say which state they mean. Two of the distractors assign the layer to somebody. A later campaign on a canvas may be the painter, a restorer, a copyist, a dealer or a thief, and the report does not say, so a description of the material is not a description of the hand. The other two are inferences in the wrong direction. A hidden passage does not imply an unfinished picture; it implies only that the picture was finished and then covered. And a figure standing out against a flat sky is what a figure that was always there looks like when the covering is gone, not what a repainted one looks like; to claim a later hand one would want evidence from the paint itself, and the report gives evidence of coverage, not of a second execution. The test: ask what would have to be found in the paint layer to support a claim about authorship, as against a claim about sequence.
questions.hint: Ask what the report establishes about sequence, and what it does not establish about who applied the layer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A dated inscription and two lamps on a court carpet
questions.learningObjective: use a date and a design irregularity as two kinds of evidence
questions.stem: An entry for a carpet reads: Safavid Iran, dated 946 in the Muslim calendar, equivalent to 1539 to 1540; wool pile knotted on a silk foundation; about ten and a half metres long and five and a half wide; a yellow central medallion on a dark blue ground with sixteen pointed oval pendants; a lamp hanging from each end of the medallion's axis, and the two lamps are of different sizes; quarter medallions in the four corners; the ground covered by two superimposed systems of spiralling stems; a main border of blue with red cartouches separated by large green rosettes; about 5,300 knots in every ten square centimetres. What has the entry established?

options.text: That the unequal lamps are a later repair, since a pair of lamps in a symmetrical design ought to match and a difference must follow a change
options.misconception: assumes a symmetry rule that the design does not follow

options.text: That the carpet was made for a floor, since a size of ten and a half by five and a half metres leaves no other surface on which it could be laid
options.misconception: infers a function from a dimension that suits several uses

options.text: That the carpet carries a date from its own inscription, and that the unequal lamps are a feature of the design, so both are evidence of the object's own account of itself
That the carpet was woven in a place named in the inscription, since a maker's signature on a carpet is a statement about where he worked
options.misconception: reads a personal name and a date as a statement of place

questions.explanation: Two of the most useful things in a catalogue entry are here, and they are different in kind. The date is on the object. A short inscription at one end gives a year in a calendar, a line of verse and a personal name, and that is an unusually direct piece of evidence about when a textile was finished, arrived with by a small group of carpets whose inscriptions put them within a few years of each other. The unequal lamps are a design fact, and this is the interesting case, because the obvious reading is wrong. The design is otherwise symmetrically balanced, and the two lamps along the central axis are deliberately unequal, which means either that a perspective was intended, in which case the design is showing the lamps as they would appear from a seated position, or that a deliberate irregularity was allowed into an otherwise perfect scheme. The one explanation to avoid is a repair, because a pair of lamps is a design and not a component, and a difference in the size of a woven motif is not what a repair looks like. Two more things to keep apart. An inscription giving a name and a date is not a statement about a place of production, and the knot density is a statement about labour and quality rather than about use. The test: for each line of the entry, ask whether it is a claim about time, about the design, about the labour, or about the use, and keep the four apart.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A numbered panel from a set of casta paintings
questions.learningObjective: explain what a labelled grid of scenes is doing in a picture
questions.stem: A painting of about 1775, oil on canvas, now in a museum in the United States, is one of a complete set of sixteen by a painter who arrived from Spain and worked in Mexico City. Each panel is about 51 by 39 centimetres, and a title with a number is inscribed above the image. This panel shows a family in a domestic interior: a man seated in a house gown, a woman preparing a drink with a whisk in a copper pot, and a son in European dress carrying a brazier. Its inscription names a mixture and names the category it produces. What is this set doing?

options.text: Documenting, so a set of sixteen interiors is a record of how people in the colony actually furnished their houses
options.misconception: treats a set that argues a thesis as a neutral survey

options.text: Classifying, so the number, the title and the household objects together assert an order of descent, and the setting is where that order is meant to be visible
Teaching, so sixteen numbered scenes is the number of steps in a catechism and the sets were used in schools
options.misconception: matches a subject to an institution on nothing but the number sixteen

options.text: Advertising, so a set painted by a Spaniard in Mexico City was a portfolio of samples for buyers in Europe
options.misconception: infers a commercial purpose from the painter's origin and the subject

questions.explanation: The whole apparatus of the set is a claim about order, and the number is the first part of it. Sixteen panels, each with a title and a number, each showing a pairing and a result, and arranged so that the sequence runs from the pairings held to be least mixed to those held to be furthest from any purity: that is a classification presented as a sequence, and a sequence needs to be numbered or it is not one. The interior is where the classification is made visible. A family at a table, with the utensils, the clothing, the drink being prepared and the brazier carried in, is a scene in which the mixture is shown as a household, which is what makes the categories seem natural rather than arbitrary. The labels then do the work the images cannot: they name what the picture cannot show, which is a rule. Three errors to reject. A set like this argues a thesis and is not a neutral survey; the objects are chosen because they fit the argument about domestic order, and they are a genre with a purpose. Nor is there evidence here of a commercial portfolio, and the painter's origin says nothing about why a picture was made. And nothing connects a number of panels to a number of steps in a catechism. The test to apply: ask what a viewer could learn from a single panel, and then what the sixteen together add, and the second question is where the meaning of the set is.
questions.hint: Ask what a single panel cannot say, and what the sixteen numbered panels add together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The painter who includes himself in a court portrait
questions.learningObjective: account for a self-portrait as a statement about hierarchy
questions.stem: A Mughal album page of about 1615 to 1618, in opaque watercolour, ink and gold on paper, shows an emperor seated on an hourglass, a gold sun-and-moon halo and flames of gold around his head. He turns away from a line of four bearded men, the first of whom is a Sufi holy man with bare hands receiving a book in his shawl, followed by an Ottoman sultan with his palms together and two kings. At the end of the line, much smaller, stands the painter in a plain robe, bowing, holding a small painted sheet. The margins are of a later date and carry inscriptions. What is the painter's inclusion doing?

options.text: Fixing a hierarchy, since the painter's own small bowed figure records his place in a scale of spiritual and political rank, and only a painter could put himself at the bottom of it
Rejecting the commission, since a painter who shows himself diminished has disowned the work and the emperor will not have it
options.misconception: infers a refusal from a figure's smallness

options.text: Signing the work, since a painter who appears in his own picture is identifying the sheet in the only way available to him
options.misconception: reads a self-portrait as a signature

options.text: Adding an allegory, since a small figure holding a picture in a court scene is a standard emblem of the art of painting
options.misconception: substitutes a general emblem for a specific, datable act of self-presentation

questions.explanation: The scale of the figures is a scale of rank, and the painter has put himself on the bottom rung of it deliberately. The seated emperor is the largest and is the only figure with gold on him; the holy man is nearly as large and is the only one the emperor actually engages with; the Ottoman sultan and the two kings are smaller and stand in a line; the painter is smallest, at the end, bowed, and holding a small painted sheet. That is a claim about a scale of spiritual and political worth, and it is being made by the man whose standing in it is lowest. The self-presentation is the interesting part, because it is not a boast. A painter who places himself at the end of a line of kings has recorded the hierarchy as he understood it, and the recorded hierarchy is the one in which a painter sits. The minute sheet he holds is the sign of that trade. The sheet is also a technical device, since the small painting within the painting shows the same kind of work, and the fact that he is shown holding a masterpiece rather than a commission is a piece of flattery a court painter could hardly avoid. Two of the distractors misread the act. Including himself is not a signature, since the sheet in his hand is plainly a picture and not an inscription, and a signature is an inscription. Nor is a small figure a refusal; a picture of this kind was made for the patron, and it is present. The third answer, about an emblem, is a generalisation from a detail that here has a specific and datable meaning. The test: ask what would change in the picture if the painter had painted himself at the same size as the kings.
questions.hint: Ask what the painter's own scale in the group is asserting, and why only a painter could assert it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An album of twenty-five leaves of everyday life
questions.learningObjective: evaluate an album's claim to be a record
questions.stem: A museum note reads: an album of twenty-five leaves by a court painter of the late eighteenth century, in ink and light colour on paper, each leaf about 22 by 27 centimetres, with the artist and the date written on several leaves. The subjects are the daily occupations of common people: a wrestling match, a forge, a library, a ferry crossing, a civil examination, a laundry, a physician at work, a travelling fortune-teller, a scholar's room. Most leaves have no background at all, the figures arranged against the plain paper. What has the note established?

options.text: That the album is a sketchbook, since leaves without backgrounds and in light colour are studies rather than finished pictures
options.misconception: infers a working state from a convention of plain grounds

options.text: That the subjects are low, since a court painter who chose common people was working outside his commission
options.misconception: reads subject matter as a measure of status

options.text: That the leaves are a complete survey, since a set of twenty-five occupations drawn by a court painter was made to record the whole of a society
options.misconception: treats a selective set with a viewpoint as an exhaustive record

options.text: That the leaves are dated documents of a specific period, and that the plain grounds concentrate attention on the figures, while the record remains a selective one

questions.explanation: There is a real document here and a real argument, and they need to be kept apart. The document is the inscription: names and dates on the leaves mean the set was made over a period by a painter who was paid, named and thinking about time, and that is why it can be placed. The dated record is also a selective one, and that is the point worth pressing. Twenty-five occupations chosen by a person with a particular training, a particular patron and a particular eye is a set of choices, and a set of choices tells you at least as much about the chooser as about the chosen. Some occupations appear and others do not, and the ones that do not are as informative as the ones that do. The plain grounds are the other thing the note establishes, and they are a formal decision. With no setting behind them, the figures have to be arranged by their own bodies and their own actions, so each leaf turns into a small solution to the problem of showing a piece of work as a piece of work, and the eye has nowhere to go but the action. Three errors to reject. A selective record is not a complete survey, and a court painter's set of common occupations is a choice with a patron in it. Nor is a plain ground evidence of a working state; it is a finished convention that concentrates the subject. And the last is a non sequitur: subject matter is not a measure of an artist's standing, and this painter's standing in part rests on having made this album. The test: ask which occupations are absent, and what the absences are about.
questions.hint: Ask which occupations are absent from the album, and what the absences are about.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The mirror and the doorway in a picture about looking
questions.learningObjective: sequence the reading of a picture built around the act of looking
questions.stem: A painting of 1656, oil on canvas, now in the Museo del Prado, shows a painter standing at a large canvas in a room in a palace, with a palette and brushes in his hand, a young princess with two attendants behind her, a small dog, two dwarfs, and at the back a large dark mirror on the wall reflecting two figures standing side by side, and further back an open doorway with a man standing in it. First say what the mirror and the doorway are doing to the problem of who is looking, and then say why the painter's own presence is not incidental to either.

options.text: They confirm the subject, since two figures in a mirror at the back of a royal room can only be the king and queen
options.misconception: accepts a conventional identification of a reflection as a documented fact

options.text: They date the picture, since a mirror and a doorway used together in this arrangement belong to a single decade in the practice of this palace
options.misconception: invents a datable convention from a compositional combination

options.text: They offer three positions for the viewer, and the painter at his canvas is the term that connects them, since he is looking at what we are looking at
They remove the viewer from the picture, since a mirror showing two figures ends the sequence of glances inside the frame and leaves us outside it
options.misconception: treats a reflected pair as a closure rather than as one more stage of looking

questions.explanation: The painting is a machine for producing a position for the viewer, and it has three positions and it cannot settle on one. The mirror at the back shows two figures side by side, standing where the viewer stands, and it is placed on the back wall so that the reflected pair is at the far end of the same axis along which we look. The open doorway behind it is a further stage: a man standing in it, small and lit from outside, looking in. And between them all is the painter, at a canvas almost as large as the picture, with his back to us, working. So the eye travels: from the princess and the court in the middle distance, to the painter's canvas, to the painter, to the mirror, to the doorway. At each stage somebody is looking at something, and at each stage the object of the looking is in the picture. That is the second half of the answer. The painter is what makes the sequence possible. A painted picture of a room is a thing in the room, and if the painter is not there the picture is a window we look through; because he is there, at his canvas, looking out at the scene we are looking at, the picture becomes a picture about the making and the receiving of pictures, and we are placed in the position of the thing being painted. That is why the brush and the palette are given to him and why the mirror is behind the princess and not in front of her. Three errors to reject. A mirror does not close a sequence of glances; it adds one. The two reflected figures are very probably a royal pair by the conventions of the office and the costume, and the identification is a strong proposal rather than a document. And a combination of devices is not a datable convention. The test: count the positions in the room from which somebody can be looking, and ask which of them the painter occupies.
questions.hint: Count the positions in the room from which somebody can be looking, and ask which the painter occupies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The tower and the harbour in a sixteenth-century panel
questions.learningObjective: connect two elements of one composition to two different claims
questions.stem: A panel of 1563, oil on panel, now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, shows a huge circular tower under construction at the centre, with cranes, scaffolding, a stonemason's yard in the near foreground, a king in a scarlet cape standing at the foot looking up, and at the left a busy harbour with ships, quays and a city stretching away. A stone tablet in the foreground carries a date and the painter's name. First say what the tower is doing in the picture, and then say what the harbour is doing.

options.text: The tower is the subject and the harbour is background, since a building under construction is a more important object than a row of ships
options.misconception: ranks two elements of a single composition by importance rather than by function

options.text: The tower is at the centre of human pride, and the harbour is the trade that pays for it, so the two halves of the panel are an argument and a cause
The tower is a portrait, and the harbour is the sitter's trade, since a man who builds and a man who sails are two subjects the panel records
options.misconception: turns a construction and a port into portraits of two occupations

options.text: The tower is a ruin, and the harbour is the sea it once reached, since both are shown at the moment when the building is finished
options.misconception: reads a building under construction as a finished structure

questions.explanation: The two halves of this panel are not two subjects; they are a premise and a consequence, and the picture's argument runs from one to the other. The tower is at the centre, enormous, and visibly unfinished, and the detail of its making is what is being shown rather than its completed state: cranes, scaffolding, the spiral of the ramp, the courses of stone, a mason at work, and a king in scarlet standing small at the foot looking up. That is pride in the making, drawn with a precision that lets you count the work. And then the left-hand half is the money. A quay, ships, a city, crowds, the whole apparatus of commerce, and a very different kind of activity from hauling stone. So the panel sets a mass of labour and pride against the trade that pays for it, and it does so without a word: the two halves share a scale, a light and a horizon, and the reading is supplied by the contrast. The stonemason's yard in the near foreground and the harbour at the left are also a compositional pair, one on each side of the tower, which is how the eye is given the whole of the argument. Two of the distractors get the relation wrong. It is not a matter of one element being more important than another; a panel of this size is built so that two kinds of work are visible at once. Nor is a building under construction a ruin, and the harbour is not a body of water a building once reached. The last converts a construction and a port into two portraits, which is a different kind of picture altogether. The test: ask what the left half is doing that the centre cannot do by itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the left-hand half of the panel is doing that the centre cannot do by itself.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mourning party in a boat and the many versions of it
questions.learningObjective: separate the reading of a picture from the fact of its multiple versions
questions.stem: A panel of 1880, oil on panel, now in the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin, shows a rocky island in a still, flat sea, a row of dark cypresses along the rock, a tomb among them, a standing woman in a long black robe with a white veil and a small stringed instrument, a small winged figure beside her, a standing stone coffin, and a boatman in the foreground poling a boat with his face hidden by a folded garment. Several other versions of the same subject were painted, with differences. First say what the figures in the boat are doing, and then say what the existence of several versions tells you about the picture's purpose.

options.text: The boat is a passage out, and the several versions are a commercial decision, since a subject that sells can be repeated with variations to suit a buyer
The boat is a rescue, and the several versions show the painter could not settle on a composition and kept returning to an unsolved problem
options.misconception: reads a commercial pattern as a failure to resolve a design

options.text: The boat is a funeral, and the several versions show the subject was a commission repeated for a patron who asked for it again
options.misconception: assumes a repeated commission where a market for the subject is the better explanation

options.text: The boat is decorative, and the several versions show the panel belongs to a set of pictures for one room, each with its own subject and its own boat
options.misconception: invents a decorative set from the fact of repetition

questions.explanation: Read the boat and the versions separately, because they answer different questions. The boat is a passage, and everything in the picture says so. The water is flat and without a horizon of open sea, the boatman is rowing with a slow look, the woman's hair and her veil lie in a still wind, the cypresses stand black and vertical, and the stone coffin is upright rather than lowered, which is a decision that has been prepared and not carried out. The small winged figure and the stringed instrument are quiet, not dramatic. So the boat is not a rescue and not a fight; it is a departure, and the picture is about the crossing and not about what is left behind. The versions are a separate matter and the useful thing to notice is that they vary. The proportions of the panel, the arrangement of the trees, the number of the figures, the colour and the details of the ornament all differ, and they differ in ways that suit different buyers and different rooms. A subject that can be produced in that many configurations was being produced for a market rather than for one commission, and the painter was able to vary it because the composition is a formula with adjustable parts. Two of the distractors misread the boat. A boat poled across still water with no struggle in it is not a rescue, and the last frame is not a fight. And a repeated subject is not evidence of an unresolved problem; it is evidence of a formula. The third answer is the right kind of reasoning with the wrong premise, since a repeat on this scale is a market rather than a patron's request. The test: ask what varies between the versions, and what stays.
questions.hint: Ask what varies between the versions, and then ask what the boat is actually doing.
