questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A lowered sword below a spectral figure
questions.learningObjective: account for a symbolist composition as a set of signs
questions.stem: A painting of 1876, oil on canvas, now in the Musee d'Orsay, shows a young woman standing with her back to the viewer at the right, in a richly worked garment, holding a sword whose point is turned down towards the ground, with a small vessel in her hand and her face in profile. She is placed before a high wall. Above and to the left, in a band of light, is a spectral enthroned figure whose body is a woman's and whose head is a crowned skull, and a small tadpole-like creature clings to the wall below it. First say what the lowered sword and the turned body do to the reading, and then say why the band of light and the skull are the composition's key.

options.text: They show the picture is unfinished, since a spectral figure with a woman's body and a skull for a head is a design that was not resolved before the canvas was abandoned
options.misconception: reads a deliberately hybrid figure as an abandoned design

options.text: They place the scene in a chapel, since a high wall, a band of light and a small creature are the standard fittings of a sanctuary
options.misconception: turns two symbolic elements into architectural evidence

options.text: They withhold a name and refuse a face, so the figure is read as a person who has just been refused something, and the light and the skull supply what she is refusing to look at
They name both figures, so the sword settles the woman and the skull settles the figure above, and the painting's difficulty is a matter of iconographic research
options.misconception: treats a deliberately unfixed subject as a puzzle with a discoverable answer

questions.explanation: The composition works by refusal, and both halves of the question are about what it withholds. The woman's body is turned away and her sword points down, so she is not attacking, and she is not going anywhere either; a lowered blade after a refusal is a gesture with no continuation. Her face is in profile and partly lost, so she is not identified, and the small vessel in her hand is the one object in the picture that could be given a name. Above her, and separated from her by the wall, is the enthroned figure: a woman's body with a crowned skull for a head, which is the most unstable thing in the picture, and a band of light that keeps it both present and unapproachable. So the upper group is what the lower figure will not turn round to see, and the wall is what keeps them apart. The band of light and the skull are the key because they are the only things in the picture that are not naturalistic: the light has no visible source and the skull has no body to belong to, and between them they tell the viewer that the encounter is not physical. Two of the distractors want to close the picture. A sword and a skull do not name anybody; a painter of this kind built ambiguity into the subject deliberately, and a name that has been proposed is a proposal. And a hybrid figure is not an unfinished design, since a body with a skull for a head is exactly the kind of image a symbolist painter would construct. The test: ask what the woman would have to do to look at the figure above her, and then ask why she does not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a set of sixteen numbered scenes
questions.learningObjective: sequence a classified series by the rule that orders it
questions.stem: A set of sixteen casta paintings made in Mexico City in the later eighteenth century was hung as a grid, four panels across by four down, and every panel carries a number and a title at the top giving a pairing and the category it produces. The series is ordered so that the first panel pairs a man of European descent with an indigenous woman, and the panels work down from there to pairings that move further from any European ancestry. Put these four panels in the order the series gives them.

options.text: Numbered six: a European man and an African woman produce a mulatto, the pairing the series places well down its list
Numbered sixteen: a pairing the series puts last, because it is the point at which the scheme can no longer name a result
Numbered twelve: a pairing of two people both descended from mixed ancestry, further from any European blood than the panels above it
Numbered one: a European man and an indigenous woman produce a mestiza, the pairing the series puts first and the one it treats as the least mixed

questions.explanation: The order is the argument, and it is legible from the numbering rather than from the pictures. What the series does is begin with the pairing its colonial hierarchy preferred, and in the sets most often reproduced that first panel pairs a man of European descent with an indigenous woman and names the result a mestiza. The African pairing, a European man and an African woman producing a mulatto, is placed further down, and in the sets that number sixteen it usually carries a number in the middle of the first six, never the first. From there the series works down through pairings of a European man with women who are themselves mixed, each one given a new and less familiar name, and then into pairings among the mixed themselves, until the last numbered panel is one the scheme can no longer carry further. So the sequence is a measure of distance from the European, and the measurement is the whole content of the set. Reading the numbers is therefore the way to read the set, and a viewer who reads sixteen separate domestic interiors instead gets sixteen scenes and no order. The test to apply: ask which panel a set would number first if the numbering were meant to make a claim about rank, and the answer tells you what the set is arguing and therefore how to order it.
questions.hint: Ask which panel a set would number first if the numbering were meant to make a claim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The design of a court carpet read from the centre outward
questions.learningObjective: sequence the components of a repeating design from its focus to its edges
questions.stem: A carpet woven in Safavid Iran and dated 1539 to 1540 has, at its centre, a yellow medallion with sixteen pointed oval pendants, and on the same axis a hanging lamp above and below it, one larger than the other. In each corner of the field there is a quarter of a simpler medallion without lamps. The rest of the field is covered by two superimposed systems of spiralling stems on a dark blue ground, and the whole is enclosed by a main border of blue with red cartouches separated by green rosettes, inside an inner border of cream with a floral meander and an outer border of red with a double meander. Put these five elements in the order in which the design reads from its focus outward.

options.text: The quarter medallions in the corners, which answer the central medallion at the edges of the field
The yellow central medallion, from which the sixteen pendants and the two unequal lamps are suspended
The outer border of red with a double meander, the outermost band and the last thing the eye reaches
The two superimposed systems of spiralling stems, the ground on which everything else stands
The main border of blue with red cartouches, which closes the field and begins the processions of bands

questions.explanation: A carpet is a diagram, and it is read from its focus outward in a fixed order, which is why the same design can be produced at different sizes without losing its logic. The first element is the central medallion, the largest single shape and the only one that is not a border or a field. Its sixteen pointed pendants and the two lamps on its axis hang from it, so they are read with it rather than after it. Then the quarter medallions in the corners, which are the design's answer to the centre: a reduced version repeated four times, without the lamps, so that the field is bounded at four points and the eye is closed rather than left open at the edges. Then the ground itself, the two superimposed systems of spiralling stems, which is the last thing read and the first thing seen from a distance, since it is what makes the field read as a single surface. And then the bands, which is where the eye leaves the field: the main border of blue with red cartouches and green rosettes closes the field, the inner cream band with its meander follows, and the outer red band with a double meander is the last thing reached. That order is also the order of a weaving plan, since the design would be drafted from the centre out, which is why a carpet of this size exists as a single integrated drawing rather than as a pattern cut from a repeat. The test to apply: ask which element a weaver would have to fix first, and the answer gives the order.
questions.hint: Ask which element a weaver has to fix first, and which the eye reaches last.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of blocks and printing in a colour woodcut
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a multi-block relief print
questions.stem: A colour woodblock print of 1857 from a series of a hundred views of one city shows a sudden shower over a wooden bridge, with figures running along it holding hats and umbrellas, fine parallel lines of rain across the whole sheet, a dark bank opposite with a pine and a small building, and a graded sky. Put these four stages in the order in which a sheet like this was produced.

options.text: The outlines, transferred from the designer's drawing to a cherry-wood block and printed first in black, so that every other colour has a line to sit in
Graded blocks for the sky and the water, laid in with a brush so that the tone darkens across the sheet rather than stopping at a line
Printing in registration, with each colour block printed over the last and checked against the key so the sheets come out aligned
The key block, cut from the designer's reversed drawing and printed to give the structure of the picture in one colour

questions.explanation: The order runs from the line to the block to the wash to the assembly, and every step depends on the one before it. First the outlines: the designer's drawing is turned face down onto a block of cherry wood, inked and transferred, so that the printed line comes out the right way round, and the block is cut with the grain and the finest part of the design kept. The outlines are printed first, in a single dark colour, because everything afterwards has to have something to sit in; a print with no line in it has no place for the other colours to stop. Then the key block, cut from the same design but simplified to the shapes that define the structure of the picture, and printed so that the main masses are established in one colour. Then the graded blocks, cut separately and inked with a brush rather than a roller so that a tone can be laid in as a band with a soft edge, which is what gives a sky its gradation and a river its reflections; on a sheet with rain in it, the lines of rain and the graded sky come from this stage. And last the assembly: each colour is printed in turn over the last, the sheet is checked against the key, and the printer's skill is in holding the registration and in judging the pressure, since pressure differences change the line weight. The test to apply: ask what has to exist on the paper before a graded tone can be laid in, and the answer is the line.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the eye through the two zones of a Toledo altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: sequence a two-zone composition from its lowest register upwards
questions.stem: The order in which the eye is taken through a tall canvas painted in 1586 to 1588 and still in its church in Toledo, which shows a funeral in a church interior at the bottom of the picture, with mourners, clergy, a sarcophagus and a small angel, and a long narrow heavenly zone above in which a small figure is carried upward, saints stand at the sides, and above them a central group of heaven is held within clouds and instruments. Put these four parts in the order in which the eye is taken through the picture, from the bottom upwards.

options.text: The clouds and the instruments above the saints, which close the picture at its top edge
The small figure leaving the tomb and beginning to rise, which is the hinge between the two zones
The heavenly zone, a long and dark band in which a small figure is carried upward and saints stand to either side
The church interior, in which a body is being laid in a tomb before a crowd of ordinary proportions

questions.explanation: The order is bottom to top, and it is the order of a soul leaving a body. First the church interior, because a viewer stands below and the lower zone is at their own height: a body being laid in a tomb, a crowd of mourners in ordinary proportions, clergy, a sarcophagus, a small angel about the size of a child, and at the edge the painter himself with his hand on the tomb. Then the hinge, the small figure that has left the tomb and is beginning to rise, which is the one passage in the picture that belongs to both worlds at once, since it is still small and is already airborne. Then the heavenly zone, which is a long dark band in which saints stand to either side and the rising figure is carried higher, with everything in it drawn longer and thinner than the figures below so that the space itself has changed. And then the top, the clouds with the instruments of the Passion, which close the picture and are placed where a viewer leaving the chapel passes them last. So the reading is a single ascent, and it is why the proportion change in the upper zone is applied systematically rather than to one figure. The test to apply: ask where a viewer's eye is when they enter the chapel and where it is when they leave, and the composition should answer.
questions.hint: Ask where a viewer's eye is on entering the chapel and where it is on leaving.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the colours of the Potato Eaters are the argument
questions.learningObjective: explain a palette as a claim about a subject
questions.stem: Explain why a painting of 1885, oil on canvas, now in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, was built almost entirely out of dark earth colours, and say what that does to the meal it shows.

answer.exemplar: Begin with what the picture is: five people around a table under a single hanging lamp, in a dark room, eating potatoes from a shared dish, and the hands and faces are large in the field and the light falls on the food and on them. Then set out the palette, because it is the claim. The browns, the greens, the ochres and the greys are all of the earth, and the light itself is a lamp flame, which is a warm but very small light in a very dark room. So the picture is entirely the colour of the ground it is about. That is not a failure of skill and it is not a stage in a process; a painter who could paint a brighter picture has chosen this one, and the choice was made in a letter to his brother in which he described eating a plate of potatoes in the evening and said he wanted to show people eating potatoes. The consequence is that the meal becomes the subject rather than the pretext. There is no wine, no luxury, no silver, no game; there is a dish of potatoes, a pot, coarse bread, and hands. The plainness is a moral claim about what is worth painting and about who eats. Then work out why the hands matter so much. They are the lightest and warmest things in the picture, they are painted with a thick and searching touch, and they are at the centre of the composition, so the act of eating is the event the light has been brought to. The faces are turned, crowded and not idealised, and each one is a different age and a different expression, which is the opposite of a unified allegory. Now the two errors to close. The first is that this is an early, unsolved picture superseded by a later, brighter style, and that is simply a fact about the painter's biography and not about this picture: it is finished, it is consistent, and its darkness is doing work. The second is that the dark palette is a symbol of despair, and that is a reading imposed on the picture; the people are eating together, the lamp is lit, and the claim is about solidarity and about subject matter, not about mood. The test to apply: ask what would be lost if the lamp burned brighter, and the answer is most of what the picture is arguing.

questions.explanation: This question is about a palette doing the work of an argument, and the method is to start from what is observable and then ask what the choice costs. The observable facts are narrow: a low range of dark earth colours, a single small light source, five figures at one table, a shared dish, and hands and faces large in the field. From those, the question of what the palette is for is answerable, and the answer has to be argued from the picture rather than borrowed from a letter the painter wrote. The useful move is to ask what would be lost if the lamp burned brighter, because that identifies the palette as a decision rather than as a limitation or an early stage. The second move is to distinguish a claim about subject matter from a claim about mood, because a good answer should notice that the picture shows people eating together, which is not the same as showing them in despair. The third is to handle the two standard dismissals: that this is an immature picture superseded by a later style, and that the darkness stands for something psychological. Both are arguments from outside the canvas, and both fail the test of asking what the object itself is doing. The last move is the generalisation worth leaving, that a limited palette is a way of excluding, and that the exclusion is usually the point.
questions.hint: Ask what would be lost if the lamp in the middle of the room burned brighter.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The glass and the curtain in a double portrait
questions.learningObjective: account for the devices that make a picture about seeing
questions.stem: Explain what a tall glass cylinder standing on the table between two richly dressed young men, and a curtain hanging across the upper left of the picture, are doing in a portrait painted in 1533, and say what they add to the objects on the shelf.

answer.exemplar: Take the two devices first and then the shelf, because that is the order in which they work. A tall glass of clear water or wine standing upright on a table has one property that nothing else in the picture has: it refracts. A viewer looking through it sees the room inverted and narrowed, so an object that would otherwise be a still life becomes a lens, and the picture quietly announces that it is made of optics. A curtain drawn across the upper left is the second device. It interrupts the view, it is the only soft-edged mass in a picture of hard surfaces, and it hangs at the level of the men's heads, so it marks the space between the wall and the viewer's side of the room. Together they say something simple and important: this picture is about looking, and about the fact that the viewer is somewhere specific and outside the frame. The two are also complementary. The glass makes the world legible but reversed, and the curtain makes it partly unavailable, and the two together keep the eye moving between what it can and cannot resolve. Now the shelf, which is the picture's other argument. A terrestrial globe, a small book, an image in a case, a lute, a case of flutes, dice, a rosary, a bell and a cross are not a list. Each opens a subject, and together they open learning, music, devotion, travel, fortune and mortality, and several of the objects also carry puns on the two young men's names. The glass and the curtain are what allow the shelf to be read as a proposition rather than as a display, because they tell the viewer that this is a constructed scene of looking rather than a description of a room. Two errors to close. The glass is not there to show the quality of the wine or the wealth of the table, and neither device identifies the sitters' beliefs; these are learned devices in court portraiture and they are doing something about the act of seeing. Nor is the curtain a way of softening a hard picture, since it is a measured interruption placed to mark a limit. The test to apply: ask what each device does that a plain rendering of the same object would not do.

questions.explanation: The method for this question is to classify the elements before interpreting any of them, because a painting of this kind mixes three different kinds of thing: objects that are part of the sitter's world, objects that are part of a learned pictorial vocabulary, and devices that act on the act of looking itself. A good answer should say which category each named element falls into and then draw a different conclusion from each. The optical quality of the glass is a case in point, and the useful thing about it is that its effect is physical rather than symbolic, which is why it is easy to overlook. The curtain is the opposite: it is a mass of soft fabric in a picture of hard surfaces, and its position matters more than its texture. The shelf then needs a third kind of argument, of the kind that turns a list into a proposition, and that argument has to be made item by item rather than asserted in general. Two errors to close: reading the objects as evidence of what the sitters owned or believed, and treating a soft curtain as a decorative softening of a hard picture. The test to apply: ask of each element whether removing it would change what the picture is doing, and discard the ones that would not.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two devices does that a plain rendering of the same object would not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a man shown from behind can carry a landscape
questions.learningObjective: explain the back-turned figure as a device that lends a viewer the mountain
questions.stem: Explain why a landscape painted about 1818, oil on canvas, now in the Hamburger Kunsthalle, puts a single man in the near foreground with his back to the viewer, standing on a rocky height above a sea of fog out of which a few rocky peaks rise, and say how that figure and the fog divide the work between what can be known and what cannot.

answer.exemplar: Begin with what the figure does, because everything else follows from it. He is seen from behind, close to the front of the picture, and he occupies the near third of the field standing on rock, and the whole of the landscape beyond him is a sea of fog with a handful of peaks coming out of it. A figure seen from the back is a figure who cannot be read: no expression, no gesture towards anything, no age, no occupation beyond a coat and a stick. So the face that would tell a viewer what to feel about the view has been deliberately removed, and what is left is the position. That is the device. The man is not a person in a landscape; he is a stand for the person looking at it, and because he is looking out of the picture in the same direction as the viewer, the viewer is lent his eyes. This is the opposite of the classical landscape with a repoussoir of figures grouped at one side and a shepherd pointing at the distance, which is a picture about two kinds of people. Here there is one person and he is doing nothing except standing and looking, which makes the looking the subject. Now the fog, and this is the second half of the question. The peaks emerge from it and go no further. Nothing in the painting tells the viewer what lies behind the near ridges, how wide the valley is, or where the river runs, because the fog is doing exactly what fog does, which is to occupy the middle distance and refuse the eye a floor. And a landscape that is mostly fog is a landscape that is mostly not painted. The division of labour is therefore sharp. Below, in the near zone, everything is knowable: rock, a tree or two, a hard contour, the figure's own clothes. Above, in the middle and far distance, nothing is knowable and the peaks are isolated in a white field like specimens on a page. That division is not a failure of invention; it is the reason the man is standing there. He has climbed to a place where the ground stops, and the picture is about the moment when the ground stops. Three errors to close. The first is to read the man as a hermit, a Romantic genius or a pilgrim, which supplies a biography the painting refuses to give: he has no face and no attribute, and a stick is a walking stick and not a symbol. The second is to read the fog as a compositional trick to avoid painting detail, which inverts cause and effect, because the fog is the subject and the detail is what survives despite it. The third is to treat the peaks as a view of a particular range, which nothing in the picture supports. The test to apply: ask what the picture would lose if the figure were removed, and then ask what it would lose if the fog were painted as rock.

questions.explanation: This question is about a device and about a division, and the method is to establish what the picture withholds before interpreting what it shows. The first withholding is the face: a figure seen from behind has no expression, no gesture, no age and no story, so the one thing that would tell a reader how to feel about the view has been deliberately removed. What replaces it is position, and position is the whole of the device, because a viewer is lent the man's eyes when he looks the same way the viewer is looking. The second withholding is the middle distance, and it is a different kind of omission: it is not withheld from the picture but from the world, and the fog is what does the withholding. That gives the work a clear structure of known and unknown, and a good answer should name both halves, because the point only appears when the near zone is contrasted with the far one. The answer also has to close three tempting misreadings, and the pattern is the same in each: they all supply content the picture refuses. A biography for the figure, a motive for the fog, and a location for the peaks are all additions, and a strong answer will say what evidence each would need and note that none is present. The test to apply is to ask which single element, if removed, would cost the picture its argument, and then to ask why that element is the one that was kept.
questions.hint: Ask what a face would have told you, and then ask what the middle distance is withholding.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The self-portrait claim about a prophet fresco
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a familiar self-portrait claim against what the fresco offers
questions.stem: A fresco painted between about 1508 and 1512 on the ceiling of a chapel in Rome shows a seated prophet holding a large book, with his head turned sharply to one side, his eyebrows raised and the muscles of his neck standing out, and the whole body twisting. It has long been described as a self-portrait of the painter. Evaluate that description and say what evidence would be needed to establish it.

answer.exemplar: Start with what the fresco offers, because the description has to be tested against the object and not repeated. What it offers is a specific and unusual pose: a head turned away from the direction of the body, raised brows, a neck in tension, and a twist through the torso that is not a restful seat. That pose is doing work. A prophet in this series is about to speak, and the turn is a body about to turn to an angel, so the painting is about a person listening and preparing to answer, and the strain is the meaning. Everything else follows from that. The book is closed or nearly closed, the figure is compressed into a corner of the ceiling's architecture, and the whole scheme is the opposite of the easy, ample, frontal figure of a much later kind. So the fresco's first claim is about a manner, not about the painter. Now the self-portrait claim. It is not baseless, and there are two things behind it. A painter who puts himself into a series of ancient prophets is doing a particular kind of thing, and there are other places in the same ceiling where the identification of the artist is argued from features and from the near presence of the artist's own family. And the pose is the kind of thing a sculptor or painter would find worth recording about himself, since it is a pose that had to be solved, with the neck, the brows and the direction of the turn all worked out. But the claim has never been established by a document, and it is a claim of resemblance, which is the weakest kind of evidence. So the correct evaluation is neither to accept it nor to dismiss it. State it as a hypothesis with a specific basis, note that resemblance between a figure in a fresco and the face of its painter can be argued from a handful of features and can be argued just as easily in the other direction, and ask what would settle it. The test to apply: ask whether the identification rests on a document, on comparison with securely identified work, or on resemblance alone. In this case it rests on the third, with some support from the second, and that is worth saying out loud. Two errors to close. The first is to treat the claim as settled because it is famous and widely repeated, which is a fact about a literature and not about a fresco. The second is to dismiss it because it is unproven, which would leave a documented artistic habit unexplained and would mistake an open question for a false one. The general rule the case illustrates: a self-portrait is an attribution claim, and it needs the same evidence as any other.

questions.explanation: The question is a training case in the difference between a claim and a report of one, and the answer should be built as a test rather than as a verdict. Lay out three grades of evidence for an identification: a document that names the figure, a comparison with other work whose authorship is not in doubt, and resemblance between a face on a wall and a face on a panel. Then place the claim in the third grade and say plainly what follows. It follows that the claim is not baseless, because a self-portrait is a recognised habit and the pose is the kind of difficult thing a maker might want to record; it follows that resemblance is weak, because a handful of features can be read in either direction; and it follows that the question stays open, which is a statement about the evidence and not a verdict against the claim. A strong answer will also observe what the fresco is doing independently of any identification, since the pose, the closed book and the compression into the corner of the architecture are all legible without knowing who the figure is. The two failures to avoid are treating a widely repeated claim as thereby settled and treating an unproven claim as thereby false, and both are errors about the status of claims rather than about the fresco.
questions.hint: Ask whether the identification rests on a document, on comparison, or on resemblance alone.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Knots per square metre on a court carpet
questions.learningObjective: convert a stated knot density into a count for a larger area
questions.stem: A catalogue entry for a court carpet records an average of 5,300 knots in every 10 square centimetres of pile. How many knots does that density correspond to in one square metre? Give the whole number.
questions.explanation: The conversion is a two-step scaling and it has to be done in the right units, which is where this is usually lost. One square metre is 100 by 100 centimetres, and 100 by 100 is 10,000, so a square metre contains 10,000 square centimetres and therefore exactly 1,000 blocks of 10 square centimetres. Each block carries 5,300 knots, so the count for a square metre is 5,300 multiplied by 1,000, which is 5,300,000. The second route gives the same figure independently. First take the density per single square centimetre: 5,300 knots in 10 square centimetres is 530 knots in 1 square centimetre. Then multiply by the 10,000 square centimetres in a square metre: 530 multiplied by 10,000 is 5,300,000. The two routes agree, and the reason they must is that the only operation in both is a scaling of area by a factor of 10,000 in each case, 5,300 times 1,000 and 530 times 10,000 being the same product written twice. The number is worth computing rather than estimating because it is the figure that explains what a carpet of this kind is. Five million knots per square metre means that any area a person can see at arm's length is built from millions of separate knots, each about the size of a grain, and that density is what permitted the design to carry fine curved stems, small blossoms and the sharp points of a medallion. The carpet itself is about 10.5 metres by 5.3 metres, and by the same arithmetic its field contains roughly 295 million knots, which is the reason a pair of them is said to have taken years and about a team of ten weavers working at once.
questions.hint: Find how many ten-square-centimetre blocks fit in a square metre, then multiply the density by that number.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The width of a hung grid of sixteen panels
questions.learningObjective: compute the wall width needed for a grid of panels and gaps
questions.stem: A complete set of sixteen casta paintings is each 39.4 centimetres wide, and a museum proposes to hang them in a single row of sixteen with a gap of 10 centimetres between neighbouring panels. How wide a run of wall does that require, in centimetres? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: Sixteen panels side by side is sixteen panel widths, but fifteen gaps, because the first panel has no neighbour in front of it and the last has none behind. The panel widths come to 16 multiplied by 39.4, which is 630.4 centimetres. The gaps come to 15 multiplied by 10, which is 150 centimetres. The total is therefore 630.4 plus 150, which is 780.4 centimetres. A common wrong answer comes from counting sixteen gaps instead of fifteen, which would give 790.4 and is wrong by a whole gap, so the second route is worth doing as a check. Write the run as three repeats of a panel-plus-gap followed by a final panel: each repeat is 39.4 plus 10, which is 49.4, three of those is 148.2, and adding the last panel at 39.4 gives 187.6, which is not 780.4. So that decomposition answers a different question and the two must not be confused: the 187.6 figure is the width of a grid four panels across with three gaps of 10 centimetres, that is 4 multiplied by 39.4 plus 3 multiplied by 10, and it is the width a single row of four would need, not sixteen. The sixteen-panel run is five times four columns, and 187.6 multiplied by 5 is 938, which is neither number, because five columns of four need four inter-column gaps as well and cannot simply be stacked. The arithmetic that matters is the first one: a sequence of n items with n minus 1 gaps. The practical point is the reason a curator asks. A run of 780.4 centimetres is over seven metres, and a wall of that length changes how a set like this is hung, since the numbers on the panels are meant to be read in sequence and a viewer seven metres from one end cannot follow the order. That is why four by four is the arrangement the sets are usually reconstructed in, and why the question of the number of gaps between items is not a technicality.
questions.hint: Count the gaps as one fewer than the number of panels: sixteen widths and fifteen gaps.
